Messages.Author: Orpheus
Messages.Body:
Well, since this week tournie, on the italian forum and right here, the
question of deals arises again.

From all the discussions I hear, it looks like many people are disgusted of
the importance it takes in the game, and would like to find a solution to
avoid the worst players from ruining a table from a VP.

My question to LSJ and staff is very simple : do you plan to legifere the
deals in any way (including forbidding them, or making a one-line rule, or a
20-pages notebook...) in the time to come ? Or to let the situation
deteriorate until all tournaments are shit and more good players get bored
away from the game ?

-----------------

Until we flower."

Sunday, I asked for a deal in my first game. It is, for me, one of the few
cases where it is a logical conclusion : I had 2 VPs, a predator who could
make some bleeds, and Beast and friends as a prey. I dealt a "you kill prey
and then withdraw" with Beast because I had no hope of killing him before he
seriously maimed all my minions, and that could have benefited either him or
my predator. Beast on the other hand would probably not have survived if I
had bled a lot and then died to my prey. So we withdrawed because both our
decks were strong enough to counter each other.

What I despise *a lot* is when people withdraw because their decks are to
weak to win VPs, but still destroy the table (I still recall a Shambling
doing his work for his prey, left me vomiting on the table...).

Or when it stops good game and makes it become shit. Which is way too often.

> I would like a serious revision of the "rules" about deals.

"There are no rules about deals". LSJ. ;-)

Possible, very easy rules (cumulative or not) :

- No deals can be made involving giving VPs to another player
- A player must optimize his VPs, no matter if he still has the Game Win
- A player must optimize his VPs at any given time, even to the point of
breaking any deal made in other circumstances : if these circumstances are
changed in any way, the deal is de facto considered invalid.
- There can be no deals involving material benefits of any sort, including
money, splitting the price, going to bed with anyone, or getting a signed
picture of LSJ in a wet swimsuit. ;-)
- There are no deals. This is the Jyhad. Kill or die.

Messages.Author: Trey Morita
Messages.Body:
On Tue, 28 Sep 2004 22:26:32 +0200, Tetragrammaton <no...@usa.com> wrote:

> Orpheus wrote:
>> Well, since this week tournie, on the italian forum and right here,
>> the question of deals arises again.
>>

Rather than trying to legislate deals, why don't you try handling deals
in a different way as a player? In the DC playgroup, we almost never make
any kind of table-split deals, and that may be because we all know that
deals are not set in stone, and people can and will break deals. Once
deals become less of a sure thing, then table splitting deals should
become less common, simply because what is the point of making a deal
that you know will be broken?

Instead of sweeping deals that determine the outcome of the game, we
make deals about situations that can be resolved immediately or within
a turn, and rarely involve giving someone a VP. The following types
of deals tend to occur often:
"You rescue my vampire and I'll rescue yours, that way there is less
chance the rescues will be blocked."
"You vote for this Kine Resources Contested and I'll call the next one
with 3 points to your prey."

A lot of times we will simply rely on enlightened self-interest instead
of deals:
"I think you should rescue my vampire because all I'm trying to do right
now is survive and deny your prey a VP."
"You can block this hunt if you want but I'm just trying to gain pool
and be a wall for you."

Quite a bit of the talking in our games revolves around manipulating
perception of who is the strongest/weakest, with everyone pointing a
finger at someone else and claiming that is the person who everyone
should be worried about.

So maybe this is just the rambling of an incorrigible deal-breaker, but
I think introducing deal-breaking into your playgroup (and maybe by
playgroup I mean, the European continent) would benefit by seeing a
reduction or elimination of table-splitting deals.

Trey
- I was the first deal-breaker in DC

Messages.Author: Andrew Daley
Messages.Body:
It short, deals can suck... but I have come accept them as part of the
game.

I will make a suggestion. Most VP deals revolve around maximising VPs
to get into the final. I propose a change to the tournament structure.

With the addition of a final-less tournament for small events I have
experienced a change in attitudes. No longer is the drive just to make
the finals, it is actually trying to get as many VPs as you can. On
top of the fact that after the usual 3 games people have to sit out
while only 5 people get to play the last game.

Why not just make tournaments 3+ round events with no finals? Use the
archon to record the scores and look up the results on a final
standing table. If there are ties for positions you use the usual
techniques to distinguish.

What do people think?

Andrew

Messages.Author: Curevei
Messages.Body:
>Why not just make tournaments 3+ round events with no finals? Use the
>archon to record the scores and look up the results on a final
>standing table. If there are ties for positions you use the usual
>techniques to distinguish.
>
>What do people think?

It's worth checking out.

I can already see an issue with people doing screwy things once they realize
they can't win or in trying to prevent a situation where they can't win. But,
then, people will always do screwy (and undesirable) things to manipulate the
scoring system.

Another multiplayer CCG had a similar structure as we do with the prelims and
the final table. I was constantly trying to get rid of the final table for
that game. But, that game had ways to reward multiple players such that you
might feel like you accomplished something even when not winning and that
game's final table philosophy was much more egregious as it didn't necessarily
reward success in determining who played for the tournament victory.

If the prize structure is entirely TW-based with the overall winner getting
something extra, it might work out as the people out of running for overall
victory still have an incentive to win their later games. But, the same thing
could be done now with prizes as incentives to winning each game.

I'm sure the arguments I've often heard for final tables will be brought up -
that a final table is more dramatic, that playing against your direct
competition for victory makes for a better tournament finale. Not necessarily
bad, but it's hard to argue one side when the other is never experienced.

Messages.Author: Ector
Messages.Body:
"Johannes Walch" <joha...@scram.de> wrote in message news:<cjd0a7$462$1...@stu1id2.ip.tesion.net>...

> Strange. We don´t have these problems around here ...

These problems are very common in Minsk, since the level of players
(and their decks) here is very different. Most of our players
(including myself) are newbies, and, IMHO, the main problem isn't the
newbie's frustration from the inevitable loss but his/her inability to
find the way to improve.
If I've lost due to my mistake or lack of some cards, I should avoid
making the mistake and search the needed cards. But what can I do if
several strong players decide to include my head as a part of their
agreement? The true answer is "become strong myself", but it isn't
quite obvious.
If a player feels himself strong, he or she may attempt to break the
offending deal to suggest a more appealing one, and (s)he can also
make another deal with the "sentenced to death" players. The simplest
way to make other players respect your strength is playing a rush
deck... take two Brujah precons and see others trying to make a deal
with you :)

I was not to long ago an avid defender of table splitting deals, but i
do realize that they are bad for the game. and should be reduced in
occurance.
i think with a few simple rules we could stop the rising tide of deals.

1) remove withdrawl from the game. this rule intended to let players
that used up their decks bow out of the game is only abused for
dealmaking. nobody except the dealmakers will miss this rule
2)let only vps made in game wins count for the preliminary standings and
use the vps made in losing efforts only as first tiebrakers.
so someone who won 2 rounds with 4 vps each is ranked higher than
someone who won 1 round with 4 vps,the second with 3 vps and cut a
losing deal for 2 in the final round.
3) maybe ban table splitting deals and force a "fight it out" between
the deal partners and issue warnings if someone loses these fight it out
on purpose.

just my 2 cents

stefan

I see your point... there is always an element of mystery when trying
something new. Resistance will always be there when changes are to be
made. :)

I feel that the 'tournament metagame' becomes more complicated when
you remove 'final table'. Everyone now must play for themself. Even if
a shrewed player was to examine the progressive totals round to round,
tournament points could prove to make the difference. You basically
would have to have a calculator to determine positions and if it was a
big event there would be so many outcomes to consider. It makes deals
less appealing when there is so much uncertainty... and again this
would be as the emphasis isn't in making the final table anymore as it
is now trying to win for yourself.

It equally ties in with the new scoring system, if people are that way
inclind. As for prizes, frankly over the past 18 months, the amount
provided by white-wolf has decreased and when people have to start
forking out more money for a chance to win prizes they opt for free
tournements. Though I must confess I would pay for prizes as I like a
competative environment.

My final point I want to raise is that when a player travels so
distance to play, it is disappointing to only play 3 games and then
leave or sit and wait for the final to be over. I think it is fairer
to all if everyone played the same number of games. It would make for
a happier environment as everyone participating would be involved.

They are just my ideas... I honestly believe there does need to be
some sort of change as the vp dealing is an unwanted aspect to our
game. There will always be someone trying to abuse the system, lets
just make it harder for them! :)

Andrew

No rules affecting deals are required, deals are very important in
the game, you can't just provoke the entire table and get away with
it. The will make a deal to go against you.

I am talking about deals which go for 1-3 rounds in the future, not
the kind of deals that some people do at the beggining of the game,
like in a 4-meth game where the 2 meths make a deal from the begining
of the game to oust the 2 others and then solve their differences 1 on
1, these kind of deals are crap, if you ask me, and usually someone
gets screwed. I can analyse why, but i don't want to get into details.

Deals should be straight-forward and once made, everyone involved
must stick to the deal and not back out. After all we are methuselahs
involved in jyhad, but that doesn't mean we are without honor. Me and
everyone in my playgroup always keeps his word, we had 2-3 occurences
in the past, where a meth backed out from a deal, that were dealt in
the appropriate manner.

Deals can screw up the table, if a meth involved is stupid, but
because
jyhad is not for the unintelligent that is not something that cannot
be dealt with.

if meth A is unexperienced and meth B tries to lure him to screw
meth C, then meth C can simply explain to the unexperienced meth A why
he shouldn't do what meth B says, because it is not in his best
interest and will just screw the table. If a meth is just plain stupid
and cannot learn by any means to make deals that are in his interest
and always makes deals that screw the table and the game, then this
meth should be dealt accordingly and if he just can't learn to play

No need to remove deals from the game (or deteriorate them),
remove the stupid ones, whose acts are based on stupidity and anger.
Jyhad is not for the stupid, no man can be allowed to ruin a 4-5 or 6
men's game.

Finaly, above i am talking about those meths who can screw a game
out of vengeance or anger. e.g. i had to deal with the following
incident:

We are 4 meths left in a game, me (George playing a
Malkavian-presence-free states rant-sleep of reason), my prey (Kostas
playing a !Nosferatu), his prey (John playing a gangrel deck) and his
prey Petros (who is my predator and plays a Toreador-Magnum-combat
deck).
John with the gangrel deck (who is sitting opposite to me and
supposely is an ally) is screwed, 2 pool, 2 empty minions in torpor,
so he has no minions ready and only 2 pool, his predator (which is my
prey) has 4 ready minions, that means that even if i rescue one of
john's minions from torpor, he won't be able to remain in the game,
because he has no good cards in his hand (the Nosferatu had just
beaten the hell out of both his minions) and 2 pool.

So, it is my turn and john asks me to rescue one of his vampires, i
explain to him, that i only have 2 vampires ready (3 blood on 1 and 2
on the other) and 1 in torpor, so if i rescue his vampire, i will lose
1 action, 2 blood and he will be ousted anyway. He insists and i tell
him to let it go, because there is no way he can convince me to rescue
one of his vampires and screw myself and my chances of wining the
game.

I had a good chance to win the whole table even with my prey
ousting John, that is because i knew how Kosta's !Nosferatu deck
performed in combat, he had played that deck many times before and i
knew what to expect. I also knew how the Toreador-magnum predator of

asheaps i was sure that the !Nosferatu would get beaten by the
Toreador-magnum (my predator), i would oust him and then the Toreador
would be an easy prey for me, if i could just convince Kostas (the
!nosferatu who was my prey, to attack the Toreador).
I had no trouble convincing the !Nosferatu to rush the Toreador's
minions in every possible way (after he had ousted the Gangrel-john),
in return i promised not to attack him for 2-3 rounds and try to send
the Toreador's Alexandra to torpor. So, my plan was the following:
torporize Alexandra and diablerize her, so i would have a table vote
lock, next turn rescue Esau from torpor and play a consaguineous +
voter cap (both were in my hand) to fill esau up. Then i would be
ready to oust both the !Nosferatu and Toreador.
Because it was certain than in these 3 turns (max 1-2 more) the
!Nosferatu would get beaten up ugly, the Toreador would be weakened in
some degree and i would had been preparing to oust them both (i would
even be unharmed by the Toreador trying to defend himself with his 2
minions against the 4 of the !Nosferatu.
I only had to toast my predator's Alexandra, because he had 4 votes
and i couldn't pass a Political action without serious vote boosting
that i couldn't afford all the time (the Toreador had 2 other minions
to defend himself, had 6-7 pool and magnum at each minion, so he would
beat the Nosferatu eitherway, because i knew that that particular deck
played a dozen dodges, enough blurs and the Nosferatu played only from
long distance, no Drawing out the Beasts, only a few Terror Frenzies
all already played), Alexandra is at 1 blood, so i try to send her to
torpor with Aristotele. That is a Sleep of reason at +1 stealth
(aristotele's special), a minion of my predator (the Toreador) tries
to block with +1 intercept.

---Meanwhile, John, the beaten Gangrel, has already packed his deck
and just watches the game, waiting to be ousted by the nosferatu as he
has 2 pool and no ready minion----

I play forgotten labyrinth and get to +4 stealth, the toreador,
plays intercept and gets to +4 intercept, so i play a lost in corwds
and get to a magnificent +6 stealth, the toreador can't block so he
says "ok, i can't block, i have no more intercept", i am
delighted..... and then the asshole-John (which is also a good friend
of mine) screws the table, he taps his rumor mill and his KRCG,
burning 1 pool and gives his prey!!!! +2 intercept to block me and he
does, i play majesty. !!!!!!!!!!

In a few words, the asshole-John gave +2 intercept to his prey!!!
just to get back to me, because i refused to rescue a vampire of his
from torpor, because it was meaningless, he wouldn't be able to defend
himself eitherway.

I call this screwing up the table...

"Anger leads to the stupid side" of jyhad, leave anger and revenge
out of jyhad. Don't act like mortals do, act like the methuselahs you
are.

i

deals.
>
> 1) remove withdrawl from the game. this rule intended to let players
> that used up their decks bow out of the game is only abused for
> dealmaking. nobody except the dealmakers will miss this rule

Sounds interesting. Off the top of my head I can't think of any, good,
reasons to keep withdrawals. Not when you consider the benefit of
destroying that annoying habit that some events produce...mutual
withdrawal.

Anyone got reasons for keeping it? I'd be interested to hear 'em.

> 2)let only vps made in game wins count for the preliminary standings
and
> use the vps made in losing efforts only as first tiebrakers.
> so someone who won 2 rounds with 4 vps each is ranked higher than
> someone who won 1 round with 4 vps,the second with 3 vps and cut a
> losing deal for 2 in the final round.

Seems to put a _lot_ of focus on the game win, which I am not sure is
such a good thing.

I don't like the idea of rewarding a player with results of 1GW 3VP,
0,0 over

another that gets 1GW 2VP, 0GW 2VP, 0GW 2VP.

Surely 6VP shows that my deck is consistently more competitve?

> 3) maybe ban table splitting deals and force a "fight it out" between

> the deal partners and issue warnings if someone loses these fight it
out
> on purpose.

How do you judge that a fight is lost on purpose? I can argue that I
didn't play combat card(x) in combat(y) because I was saving (x) for a
later combat(z).

Personally, I am happy to accept table splits as a neccessary part of
the game. Deal-making is a desirable aspect of the game and table
splits are an inevitable bi-product.

Also, table splits servre a purpose in that they can give players
incentive to band together and remove threats to the table.

Two players attacking a weenine vote that is trouncing the table can
negotiate a mutually beneifial outcome based on VP's. The no-split rule
could remove a good deal of the incentive to take these kinds of
actions. The neccessity of removing particularly successful decks (in
the current game) becomes a lot less clear cut.

Example:

Players A, B, C, D.

C is the threat to the table (and refuses to deal), D has the potential
to cripple C. B & A are just some "average" decks.

1.D reasons that he can cripple C such that B can oust him. By doing so
though, D will also fall to B (who will then go on to take the table).

2.Alternatively, D can go madly forward in the hopes of gaining a a VP
(A's) before dying to C (who will then go on to take the table).

A.Currently, D has the option of cutting a deal with B. I'll give you
C, you give me A and we'll withdraw (or fight it out, or whatever).

B. Also, D may choose to deal with A. I'll give you B & C if you fold.

Having no split deals available means that D is forced in to one of the
initial scenarios (1 or 2). 2 is optimal as D at least gets a VP, but
it also sucks because the the threatening deck, that the other players
in this multi-player game of subtlties, diplomacy and intrigue :)
should be working to halt, is left free to rampage the table.

Does that make sense?

I do like the suggestion (someone made) that players should always be
aiming to maximise their VP's, even after the GW is obtained. Removes
the possibility of someone just passing out VP's as they feel like it.
I know it's unlikely, but I don't like the possiblity being there, not
when it could be removed aso easily.
Cheers,
-scrote

their decks for the final.

This suggestion is offered for rather different reasons than last
year's, though. This time, the argument is that the withdrawal rule is
bad for the game because it makes it easier for VP-splitting deals to be
made.

The major argument I expect to see for keeping withdrawal is that
Brinksmanship requires it. Of course, personally I think Brinksmanship
is not a good card to have in the game (and never should have worked
outside the central-to-the-game "oust people by reducing their pool to
0" mechanic), so I'm not really swayed by that argument. The other
argument - that the threat of withdrawal forces people to try to oust
their preys - doesn't seem that substantial to me; withdrawal is very
rarely (IME) used in that way and the game does not normally (IMO) lack
incentives for ousting your prey.

Josh

not sure that removing withdrawal from the game would improve the deal
situation all that much, though

Messages.Author: Joshua Duffin
Messages.Body:
"Curevei" <cur...@aol.commetal> wrote in message
news:20040929023551...@mb-m24.aol.com...

[Andrew Daley wrote]

> >Why not just make tournaments 3+ round events with no finals? Use the
> >archon to record the scores and look up the results on a final
> >standing table. If there are ties for positions you use the usual
> >techniques to distinguish.

> I'm sure the arguments I've often heard for final tables will be

brought up -
> that a final table is more dramatic, that playing against your direct
> competition for victory makes for a better tournament finale. Not
necessarily
> bad, but it's hard to argue one side when the other is never
experienced.

Yes, quite so. I do think it's true that having a final table is more
dramatic, and fun for (a) the finalists (well, assuming that they're not
burned out on playing finals by how final-playing tends to work) and (b)
the spectators, since you get to have the dramatic finish instead of
just everyone being in various games that all end at the same time.

It probably would lead to better final games, as Legbiter mentioned, to
hold the finals on a separate day from the preliminary rounds, since
people wouldn't be as mentally (and often physically :-) exhausted then.
But logistically that's not so simple, since just having people come to
play for eight hours on one day is asking a lot of time commitment; two
days for a single tournament is probably not feasible for anything other
than major championships.

I think it might be an interesting sub-approach here (at least from a
tournament-running standpoint) to try some kind of Swiss system for
tournaments, where each round players would be seeded by standing
against other players with the same kind of record. This would lead to
a de facto finals table at some point, and would make it so that players
who are totally out of the running wouldn't so much be able to "mess up"
the results in games that might determine the winner of the tournament.
There are problems, though: one, it would probably be possible for some
players in the "de facto finals" to already be mathematically unable to
win the tournament while playing the final game (so they *would* end up
lacking incentive to "play to win"). And two, seeding players this way
would mean that you'd play games (except at really large tournaments)
against the same opponents several times, especially if you're on the
"winning" tables. That would probably reduce the fun of the
repeated-opponents players.

But overall, I think trying a "no finals, just three-round standings"
(or four-round standings) approach might be worthwhile, sure. Another
advantage of doing it in three rounds (with no "final" fourth round) is
that the players wouldn't be as fatigued when playing their last game of
the day...

Josh

>against other players with the same kind of record. This would lead to
>a de facto finals table at some point, and would make it so that players
>who are totally out of the running wouldn't so much be able to "mess up"
>the results in games that might determine the winner of the tournament.
>There are problems, though: one, it would probably be possible for some
>players in the "de facto finals" to already be mathematically unable to
>win the tournament while playing the final game (so they *would* end up
>lacking incentive to "play to win"). And two, seeding players this way
>would mean that you'd play games (except at really large tournaments)
>against the same opponents several times, especially if you're on the
>"winning" tables. That would probably reduce the fun of the
>repeated-opponents players.

I don't think seeding players can work. By far the most important thing should
be having players play as many different opponents as possible. One of the
things about Swiss is that you aren't supposed to ever play the same opponent.

There's not enough rounds to make sure seeding actually balances anything.
Success is punished, which is good for people who don't start out well but
doesn't seem fair. I'm sure more problems can be found.

I'm going to ignore the whole dealbreaking element of the post since a) it bogs
things down in something subjective and b) I don't think it relates to these
critical comments above.

Dealmaking isn't necessary. Dealmaking only matters when players don't play
perfectly. Okay, that's all of the time. But, the point is that dealmaking is
contrary to good play. In good play, you help or hurt other people, as Trey
states, out of enlightenend self interest. Dealmaking, then, is a way for
people to capitalize on other players' inability to realize what is in their
best interest.

If it was possible to play with no talking whatsoever, I could see doing it and
people would have to think through their play rather than have people tell them
what they should do and have the game turn into an exercise in personality
management.

I don't think anything can be done about people making deals. If something
could be done, I'd focus on killing deals over VPs. But, as I keep saying, if
you want to have people play the game right, one way is to reward them and the
way to do that with this game is providing prizes strictly on the basis of
table wins. That doesn't completely solve the problem.

I'm actually not clear on why there's such a great problem in the European
tournaments that have been brought up recently. With such large numbers, the
need to play to win should be so high as to kill the desirability for throwing
games. My concerns are mostly on the 2-3 table tournament where throwing games
is perfectly reasonable for getting into the finals.

I've managed to get off focus. Basically, I wanted to point out that
dealmaking is a flaw in play, not some sort of necessary aspect to it.

"Curevei" <cur...@aol.commetal> wrote in message

> Dealmaking isn't necessary. Dealmaking only matters when players

> you help or hurt other people, as Trey states, out of enlightenend
> self interest. Dealmaking, then, is a way for people to capitalize
> on other players' inability to realize what is in their best
> interest.

...

> I've managed to get off focus. Basically, I wanted to point out
> that dealmaking is a flaw in play, not some sort of necessary
> aspect to it.

Wow! Suffice to say that such a view is an *incredibly* incomplete,
insufficent summary of the relationship deal-making has to the
concept of quality of play. Though I'd agree that participation in
deals can often be a sign of flawed play, were that the beginning
and end of the situation few or no good players would ever enter
into deals nor even entertain consideration of them. To the
contrary, excellent players are seen to offer and accept deals all
the time and often benefit and win by exercise. How can you
explain this and resolve it with the point of view expressed above?
I don't think you can.

Dealmaking simply involves the trading of short-term interests with
long-term ones. In short, it's offering the medium of future
considerations as currency for current services. The use of this
medium of exchange is both the practice's strength and its weakenss:
it allows two players to engage in activity to the mutual benefit
and welfare of both (at the expense of others at the table) creating
"goodness" out of thin air. But the "currency" is sometimes bogus,
potentially causing a player engaging it far more harm than good.
Like dynamite, it's a tool that can be very helpful or blow up in
your hands. It's risk-taking, hardly to be equated with "flawed
play".

Fred

Messages.Author: James Coupe
Messages.Body:
"Orpheus" <orphe...@DEADSPAM.free.fr> writes:

> NEVER !! There is absolutely no valid reason for that. And read LSJ' lips :
> "There are no rules for deals". Which is part of the problem (there should
> be rules *against* deals). But you cannot be forced to respect something
> which doesn't exist, right ?

If we assume that that premise is true (which I'm not commenting on
for now), how would you propose to rule against deals?

As LSJ pointed out recently, there are many different kinds of deals
and the ones which seem to cause most problems are the ones that are
perceived as spoiling other people's "fun, or somesuch".

Additionally, it's intrinsic to some facets of the game - politics
particularly - that deals of some kind will have to be struck. If I
don't split my KRC three to my prey and one to your prey (perhaps, on
a five player table, you're my grand-prey and he's my grand-predator),
you're going to vote it down, particularly if you're suspecting that
(say) I'm going to Cryptic Rider it. At least you get something out
of it this way.

I'll leave to one side the problem of situations where I do sacrifice
something short term, but for a similarly short term gain e.g. I'll
pass that KRC for you, even though it does hurt me a bit now, but it
lines me up for a kill on my prey. Or even "Okay, I'll give you those
votes." But... it's worth bearing in mind that some of these can be
seen as deals, and if you want to draw a line between a "deal" and
cross-table negotiation, you're going to need to start drawing general
principles for some judgement-oriented help. Where does that line get
drawn?

So, as two political decks, we're going to need to have some sort of
long term negotiations. Now, you could say that a good player would
be including Closed Session (or similar) - but that's not necessarily
the point. Perfectly reasonable situations can occur where two people
are, in fact, playing largely contradictory styles. Say, we're both
playing a 1/2 Ventrue Law Firm. We may well need to co-operate over
votes, we may well need to co-operate over who brings out which
vampires. "Hey, is that Arika? She's got nine blood on her. It's
just I have two vamps here, and one's Queen Anne and the other's Arika
and I don't want to contest or waste my transfers."

Of course, the other VLF player can lie through their teeth and try
and screw me over (or feign innocence - the "Bugger, I've been
transferring to the wrong vampire" face is worth practising). But if
he doesn't - and he's possibly of the opinion that working together
where it's mutually beneficial is better than clash of the titans -
then we have a long term negotiating point going on.

The point of all this setup is... Is that a deal that spoils other
people's fun, or is that a deal which doesn't, or is it a deal in the
first place? After all, repeated negotiation may *not* be a deal.

(The above strikes me as good play, totally valid. But that's just my
opinion.)

Would it make any difference if the two of us were playing, say,
Euro-ish-Brujah and I negotiated to bring out Donal and Anvil, and you
to bring out Constanza and Volker? Would it make a difference if we
started negotiating over which targets to take out? Perhaps you and I
are both playing the Euro-Brujah and my prey/your predator is being
particularly troublesome. Perhaps he's killing us in diablerie Blood
Hunt situations. (Perhaps we're trying to keep each other alive in
them, rather than just burning each other's vamps to mutual
destruction.) Perhaps he's brought The Slow Withering into play and
it's annoying the hell out of us and we need him gone. Or perhaps
he's just brought Recalled to the Founder into play and I want to
bring another Brujah into play, but have some weenies doing other work
for me. (If it helps, pretend it's a multi-rush deck, Fatima style,
and my weenie-types are some of the same clan as me.) I want him
dead, so I want to get rid of that vampire - but I want to know if you
can oust him next turn, or if I need to wait to bring out Volker.

Is what I've just described a deal? We really are setting out to
spoil someone else's fun now - by ousting him, with the two of us
ganging up to destroy him. But if we don't, we're going to get
screwed over a barrel.

Now, these things could be set-up as open deals. But is the
difference between a discussed long-term deal any different from a
repeated negotiation - or just two experienced players with an
unvoiced understanding, because they're both smart cookies. "Look,
he's going to kill us, right? So let's see if we can avoid that." No
explicit deal made.

So where can you rule against these "deals" in general?

> Good players don't need deals to do what they must.
>
> Bad players don't need deals to screw a table.

I think these are both invalid premises, in that they're generalised
principles which fail to take into account individual situations.

I'm on a table playing, say, a Baltimore Purge deck. Eat vampires,
destroy them. Now, this is going to incur the wrath of the whole
table most likely (save for a few ally decks, but leave that out of it
- it's very unlikely, but it's still a remote possibility). So you
could say that as a "good" player, I shouldn't have played that deck.

But, move on to a far more innocuous deck. It just happens that it's
the antithesis of my predator and prey - for a casual example, let's
say I'm playing a very fast combat deck, and they can't deal with it
at all. So they need to get me ousted. First, is that a deal from
their point of view? As the prey, I really, really, really don't care
that my grand-predator gets a VP out of this - I need that deck off
the table, RIGHT NOW.

Here, we can't really say that it's my fault per se. As a good
player, I just happened to have picked a deck and two average players
(though their skill doesn't necessarily come into it) happen to have
decks that are very vulnerable to it. So two players really need me
off the table.

It would seem churlish - counter-productive, even - to prevent those
two players from doing so. Situations in which a judge is going to
say "Yes, I know you both need this to happen. Yes, I appreciate
you're probably going to die if you don't. No, you can't do it," are
going to end with much flouncing, pouting and acrimony.

But then I, the good player, am really going to need some help to
survive. Two people battering me as hard and fast as they can is
really going to kill me. I can take one, but not two. I might want
to go to my grand-predator and point out that he doesn't want me dead,
or else his prey will have six pool more to get through. I might also
point out that with my prey going backwards a lot, my grand-prey (my
grand-predator's predator) is going to have an easy ride and be a lot
stronger at ousting him.

So, we seem to have a situation where the following things seem to be
true. (Feel free to break the assumptions if I'm wrong.)

1) As a player, I'm playing a deck that wouldn't ordinarily incur the
wrath of the entire table but which, against these players,
exploits particular holes in their decks. This might be, for
instance, an event deck (or a deck with at least some events) that
just really screws their deck a lot. (I have some reservations
about some events, but there are certainly some mostly innocuous
events that would happen to annoy certain decks. Or some master
cards that do similar - some strategy altering/hosing type cards,
say.) So it's not that I'm a "bad player" who's picked the wrong
deck. I'm a good player who picked a deck, aiming to do everything
myself.

2) It can reasonably be seen that - for my prey - it is in his
interests to have me killed. (Pick any other player on the table,
if necessary.) He needs me dead to survive. Similarly, my
predator wants me dead - perhaps for similar reasons, perhaps not.
But I now have two players who really, really, really want me dead.

I don't think that - so far - that's my fault. So I'm not being a bad
player.

I also don't think that - so far - we can really blame either of the
other players. Every deck has holes, right? You only have 90 cards,
12 or so vampires, and 7 cards in hand at once. You can't cope with
EVERYTHING properly. Some things will need to be dealt with in
different ways - like being able to destroy a vampire with a combat
deck, if you don't have bleed bounce in that combat deck, or whatever.
Creative use of what's at your disposal to deal with general
situations of badness that would otherwise kill you. Which seems
reasonable, anyway.

3) Those two players may have a deal, or they may not. In either
event, it would seem weird to have some sort of rule that stopped
them from co-operating, overtly discussed or understood, or just
simply co-operating by both killing me, even though they haven't
planned who's doing what or anything like that. It's in both their
interests to kill me, so they are playing to win. My predator
wants his VP. My prey wants to survive.

I don't think this is an uncommon situation. We've all sat down next
to a deck we just want to kill because it's destroying our ability to
play.

An alternative situation might be a Malkavian Dementation deck, going
backwards round the table. I still have two people who want me to
die, only this time there's no deal AT ALL.

4) I now have two people trying to screw me over. As a "good player"
(for the purposes of the example), am I really expected to be able
handle two decks both trying to oust me at once? Obviously, my
prey will sometimes hit back at me in any situation - but two decks
properly trying to oust me at once is a different level to that.

It seems perfectly reasonable to say that I am very likely to die.
(Sure, they could get hand jam and do unthinkably stupid things. But
it's very likely I'm going to die.)

5) If my prey isn't killing me then there's a very good chance he's
doing something wrong, because his deck needs mine to die.

Bear in mind that you didn't specify that my *prey* needed to be a
good player - just that good players don't need deals to win. So
we're both allowing for the fact that other people can be bad players,
clearly. He could've made the wrong deck.

But also, he could be a bad player in general. You can't legislate
against bad play. Perhaps he does have a way to survive that doesn't
involve going backwards at me, but there's not a hope of convincing
him of that. (Perhaps he misjudges odds, or doesn't know how likely
or unlikely something is, or doesn't realise (and can't be convinced
of) what a strong position his grand-predator, my predator, will be in
once I'm dead too, with him on six extra pool and fewer resources dead
than he should have. Whatever.)

6) But for whatever reason, I now have two people going against me.
What "good play" would you suggest I use that allows me to do what
I want that *doesn't* involve a deal. Invent any scenario you want
but the crucial points are that two other people on the table want
me dead either because my deck will neuter them/destroy them first
or one of them is my predator and the other my prey who has no
other defence to the particular strategy I've enacted. (He's got
bleed bounce, combat defence and vote cancellation, but I'm playing
nasty vampire stealing with Mind Rape or Obeah or something.) Bad
play from one of the other players involved is also an acceptable
option, or someone waiting to move in with a Dramatic Upheaval is
also a possibility, as is the Dementation back-bleed above. But if
you want to stick to people doing things for 'good play' reasons,
rather than necessarily having an off-the-wall deck, that's fine
too.

Now, there are many sorts of deal here. Obviously, getting my
grand-predator to help is a possibility (as detailed above). Or going
for threats on my prey ("I'm going to die, but I'm going to make sure
you die first") is also a sort of deal - not all deals are made
because both sides are sweetness and light about it all, but because
players are forced into it. Which can get nasty. Various threats can
go around the place, getting people to back off, help them out
temporarily, or whatever. These all result in deals of a sort -
they're just not the "Well, you do this, I do that and we both win,
isn't spring pretty and don't you look FABULOUS today, dahlink?" sort
of deal.

> But deals certainly encourage making wrong decisions and ruining some games
> for one meager VP.

It can. But what about the situations where the *right* decision is
to go with that deal? How do you propose to stop people winning
through good play?

> Deals for 1 VP should never exist : the deck making the "winning deal"
> should be able to win without the deal (if not, it would be illegal, right
> ?) ; the deck making the "losing deal" should just die painfully and not
> take the other players' potential for VPs away.

No, this isn't true in either respect. (There may be some situations
where it is - probably lots - but it's not universally true.)

The classic example of this has often been two hard combat decks
sitting next to each other. (Indeed, this was one of the situations
that brought about the Table Win rulings, based on much bitching about
such situations. The TW rule provides incentives for both of the
combat decks to want to be on the 4 side of that deal, however, which
may make the deal harder to broker.)

I have a combat deck, you (my prey) also have a combat deck. I need
to bleed through you, and to do that, I want to destroy your vampires.
(There's nothing wrong so far, this is classic rush deck stuff.)

However, to destroy your vampires, I need to go into combat. You can
hit back. You probably will hit back.

Now, assuming that we're both playing a combat deck that's largely
offense with only a little defence, it could work out that we'll
mutually annihilate each other. (The canny Gangrel fortitude player
may be in a very different situation, of course.) Say, it's two (very
different) Brujah combat decks that are going to destroy each other.
You're playing Euro-Brujah mostly, I'm doing something fun with Group
3, say. Or Brujah vs Tzimisce - we both have a little damage
prevention/avoidance floating around (e.g. Sideslip, various little
bits of Vicissitude), but we're both conscious that the deck probably
doesn't have a whole lot.

However, the specific example doesn't matter too much - we can both
find situations where combat decks next to each other will annihilate
each other. Now, if they're the last two decks on the table, it's
likely that one will last a little longer than the other and find
itself able to bleed out the other player with a copy of Hasina Kesi
over multiple turns and a well-timed copy of Fame.

But on a five player table, both of us will probably die and my
predator will destroy me, then you. 0 VPs each. And you probably
can't get a single VP because I'm killing your vampires.

So, we're both in a situation of 0 VP. (This can happen.)

If I can convince you to take the deal whereby you oust your prey,
then I sweep the table, I'm playing for a TW. You can't get a TW, so
the deal still allows you to maximise your VPs. (Of course, someone
else might be able to offer you a *better* deal - but you're not
obliged to take it, if you think they're lying etc.)

So, from 0 VPs you get 1 VP. From 0 VPs, I get a TW and 4 VPs.

Classically, it gets split 3-2 (you get the rest of the table and roll
over for me to get my pound of flesh), but various reasons might
convince you to take my deal, which is still an improvement on 0.

You don't have to take the deal, but if we allow that we're both
pretty sure we're going to kill each other (small tournament, played
each other before, single table tournament etc.) which is far from
impossible with two meaty combat decks, the deal isn't illegal.

And - as above - you try explaining to the player that he can't get a
TW that way, and has to get 0 VP instead, even though an in-game,
non-collusive piece of play allows him to do so without requiring
another player to worsen their expected outcome based on the table at
hand.

Also, hello and stuff.

--
James Coupe

Messages.Body:
Curevei wrote:

>>I was not to long ago an avid defender of table splitting deals, but i
>>do realize that they are bad for the game. and should be reduced in

Messages.Author: Frederick Scott
Messages.Body:
"Curevei" <cur...@aol.commetal> wrote in message
news:20040930050153...@mb-m16.aol.com...

> >> Dealmaking isn't necessary. Dealmaking only matters when
> >> players don't play perfectly. Okay, that's all of the time.
> >> But, the point is that dealmaking is contrary to good play.
> >> In good play, you help or hurt other people, as Trey states,

> >> out of enlightenend self interest. Dealmaking, then, is a way

> >> for people to capitalize on other players' inability to realize
> >> what is in their best
> >> interest.

> >...
> >> I've managed to get off focus. Basically, I wanted to point out
> >> that dealmaking is a flaw in play, not some sort of necessary
> >> aspect to it.
> >
> >Wow! Suffice to say that such a view is an *incredibly*
> >incomplete, insufficent summary of the relationship deal-making
> >has to the concept of quality of play. Though I'd agree that
> >participation in deals can often be a sign of flawed play, were
> >that the beginning and end of the situation few or no good
> >players would ever enter into deals nor even entertain
> >consideration of them. To the contrary, excellent players are
> >seen to offer and accept deals all the time and often benefit and
> >win by exercise. How can you explain this and resolve it with
> >the point of view expressed above? I don't think you can.
>
> First, to get it out of the way, dealmaking and cooperation aren't
> the same thing. Dealmaking is a formalization of cooperation.

Such a distinction doesn't seem meaningful. The alternative to
"formalized cooperation" - which must necessarily reference any
deals made verbally and deliberately - would be tacit cooperation,
such as a predator refraining from bleeding a prey in order to allow
him to bleed his prey (the predator's grandprey) when both clearly
view the latter as the major threat in the game. While this
happens occasionally, it's hardly worth noting for purposes of
this discussion, as far as I can see. It seems unlikely that
there'd be any confusion about such a point.

> Say you end up doing what you wanted to do in the absence of a
> deal. Then, there was no reason to have a deal to formalize
> whatever cooperation you and another player may have come up with.

Sure there is. Sometimes you can threaten an opponent with some
other behavior and affect his play, gaining you something in the
process. You can sometimes do this and gain from it because in
some situations: 1) he can't be sure that you'd decided to do what
you've chosen to do but haven't acted on yet; and 2) the deal seems
worthwhile to him given his imperfect knowledge of the state of
the game. (He may not know that, for instance, you're not holding
that Sensory Deprivation you're threatening him with and that you
possess no more of them in the deck.)

> So, a deal is only relevant when it changes behavior. But, why
> would you want to change behavior when you think you are doing
> what's in your best interests all of the time in the first place?
> On the face of it, it would seem obvious that you make deals to
> change the complexion of a game that's going against you.

Since your premise seems faulty, I assert that your conclusion is
faulty.

> You may have equal options and the way to resolve which to choose
> is by offers tendered. Except, once you assume the people
> tendering the offers are doing what is in their best interest,
> what to do should be solvable again without having to worry
> about whether a deal is in place.

Again, faulty premise ==> faulty conclusion. The attractiveness
of options will vary depending on what positive and negative
consequences are attached to each option. These, in turn - at
least sometimes - vary depending on what effects they will have
on the future behaviors of other players. Which in terms depend
on negotiations: what you can get them to agree to and/or what
each will threaten as implications of your actions. In turn
once again, this may well depend on what they reckon they can
acheive by affecting your behavior through threats and offers
in terms of their current and future behavior. "Doing what is
in their best interest" is highly dependent on the outcome of
verbal bargaining - not just the other way around.

> What is dealing but an opportunity to distort their strategy?

The question seems posed to beg a particular answer. "Distorting"
strategy, if I understand your meaning correctly, affects what is
in your best interests and the potential gain. I think you are
oversimplifying by pretending there isn't a payback loop in
operation here.

> >Dealmaking simply involves the trading of short-term interests
> >with long-term ones. In short, it's offering the medium of future
> >considerations as currency for current services.
>
> There are no short term interests to the rational player. Every
> decision has to come back to "how do I achieve my game goal?" - a
> long term interest.

I think you're mistaking my meaning here. Of course short term
interests (or "short term goals" if you will) are stepping stones
to long term interest. I meant that you sacrafice your near term
progress towards your overall goal in hopes of gaining more progress
in the long run. Or you may offer something to another player that
down the road will assist him in his long term interest (thus
ultimately harming yours at that point) in exchange for something
you need immediately that you deem more important in the long
term.

The way you're defining "short term" above is ultimately meaningless
and (deliberately or not) is an attempt to sabotage my point
through semantics. By defining it as you do, you obviate any need
to ever consider the short term vs. long term. Assuming you don't
think that's silly (and I don't think you do), the true meaning
of a player's "short term interest" and how it can sometimes be
reasonably exchanged in one direction or another with his "long
long term interest" ought to be clear.

> The point of cooperation is to help yourself. For, if you aren't
> helping yourself, why engage in the behavior. Similarly, it has
> to be assumed that a rational partner is also cooperating to
> achieve something in his or her best interests. So, why formalize
> it?

Well, for one thing you do so because clearly players are seldom
going to automatically agree on what is in one another's best
interests such that cooperation can eternally be tacit in nature.
You don't know what is in one another's libraries, crypts, and
hands (unknown information). You may each reckon differently in
terms of what third parties will do when confronted by a given
set of circumstances. Other differences in perspective.

A much BETTER reason, however, is that although the benefits of
cooperation in a certain respect may be clear to both parties, it
frequently requires each player make choices to do so at discrete
points in time. Even if the questions of trust and shared
perspective don't exist, both players still may need assurances
that the other views their cooperation in the same light and that
the nature of the mutually advantageous behavior is understood to
be the same by both parties. This is formalizing cooperation: aka
"dealmaking" by your own definition.

> You formalize cooperation because of information inequities or
> because some players aren't (always) rational. To some extent,
> the former is unavoidable as opponents won't know how you built
> your deck or what you have in hand. But, quite a bit of the
> inequity comes from the difference in ability of players to
> read the game state. By capitalizing on that difference, you
> make the formalization of cooperation relevant and produce flawed
> play on the part of the person who shouldn't have made the deal.
> And, obviously, irrational players produce flawed play.

Although I obviously agree with some of your conclusions above, I
don't agree with your overall conclusion. The issue is hardly
comes down to "flawed play" because: 1) both players may well
benefit from the cooperation; and 2) even if it turns out to be
a mistake on the part of one player due to lack of knowledge he
can't possibly have (what's in other players' deck and how each
deck is ordered), that's hardly what I would call "flawed".
Sometimes a bad deal is due to the result of a poor choice on the
part of one or even both players. I would say that isn't the
rule.

> What I'm getting at is that good play removes any need to
> formalize cooperation since it's ... good play. Having a
> deal in place to do what you should have been doing in the first
> place is redundant. Having a deal in place to do what you
> shouldn't be doing is flawed play on someone's part.

I disagree. It seems clear to me that players can and often
do increase their chances of winning through explicit cooperation
and furthermore, they do so in ways that are *not* zero sum in
nature. That is, both players increase their chances of winning
in the end. Thus, such explicit cooperation cannot be termed
"flawed".

Fred



I am somewhat surprised to see all the calls of collusion regarding this
event. Collusion means intentionally playing to the benefit of another
player in detriment of your own position.

From the description, I fail to see how this example qualifies, the
'avenging' player lost nothing by burning the 'traitor'.
In fact in most cases it is a good idea to burn a diablerist at the blood
hunt: you get rid of two opposing minions at no cost to you (and remember
that even your current 'allies' are your future prey).

OTOH, there are two main reasons not to do it: to maintain some kind of
'table balance', and to extract some kind of reward from the diablerist
later on (even if it is not formalized as a deal). If the diablerist is a
known deal-breaker, that's one less reason to keep him alive.

I think one problem is: the rules say you can only make play decisions based
on the current game, but it is unavoidable that the character of your
opponents influences your decisions. This applies to deals most clearly, but
also to other play decisions.

Flux

Messages.Author: James Coupe
Messages.Body:
Flux <fl...@netc.pt> writes:

> I am somewhat surprised to see all the calls of collusion regarding
> this event. Collusion means intentionally playing to the benefit of
> another player in detriment of your own position.

No, it doesn't.

Collusion is:

"Players agree to alter, predetermine, or otherwise illegally
establish the results of a game."

This *does not* mean that they have to play to their detriment,
necessarily. However, it can be extremely difficult to detect
collusion if it isn't in such a fashion. After all, two players
working well together to mutual benefit can look like perfectly
reasonable play, whereas if I go hell for leather to give you all my
pool and minions, it's going to be a little more obvious.

Now, the difficult thing is whether "establish the results" can be
applied to an interim thing, or just "Make that player lose" or even
"Teach that player a lesson."

The judge, of course, has discretion to rule on these things and may
feel that outside conspiring to take retribution on a player for
previous behaviour might constitute collusion.

However, a player intentionally playing to oust someone other than his
prey because (e.g.) he has a personal grudge against him of a serious
nature (stole his girlfriend, killed his dog, whatever) would, to me,
be more like Unsportsmanlike Conduct.

By extension, I would be tempted to rule that a multiple player
version of such would still be Unsportsmanlike Conduct - Major.
Example C is "refuses to play a game", this seems to be about the same
level particularly given the co-operative (even if not necessarily
collusive) nature of it.

Obviously, a given situation would demand handling it based on the
situation at the time. But, if challenged, I'd be unsure about being
able to defend a Collusion allegation, whereas I would be much more
certain of an Unsportsmanlike Conduct ruling.

--
James Coupe

Messages.Author: Frederick Scott
Messages.Body:
"James Coupe" <ja...@zephyr.org.uk> wrote in message
news:3yhdpe7...@newred.gradwell.net...
> Flux <fl...@netc.pt> writes:
>
> > I am somewhat surprised to see all the calls of collusion
> > regarding this event. Collusion means intentionally playing to
> > the benefit of another player in detriment of your own position.
>
> No, it doesn't.
>
> Collusion is:
>
> "Players agree to alter, predetermine, or otherwise illegally
> establish the results of a game."
>
> This *does not* mean that they have to play to their detriment,
> necessarily. However, it can be extremely difficult to detect
> collusion if it isn't in such a fashion. After all, two players
> working well together to mutual benefit can look like perfectly
> reasonable play, whereas if I go hell for leather to give you all
> my pool and minions, it's going to be a little more obvious.
>
> Now, the difficult thing is whether "establish the results" can be
> applied to an interim thing, or just "Make that player lose" or
> even "Teach that player a lesson."

Oh, I don't think that's a difficult choice at all! You absolutely
can NOT have players doing stuff like that in a tournament and
here's why: if people are made to feel that their chances of winning
games and tournaments are distinctly screwed over BEFORE THE GAME
EVEN STARTS, that's very bad! If your tournament environment permits
this, then it will discourage participation ("Why should I even play
if players are gunning for me before the game's even started?") for
no good reason. In the situation described (assuming it had been
a tournament, not in informal play), the "victim" would have good
reason to feel his chances of winning subsequent games were
diminished. There's no question that tournament organizers/
judges have to protect against that kind of thing.

The nebulous issue might come up if the 'punisher' had not declared
his reasons for doing what he did when he did it. Of course, had
he not done so, than the efficacy of his 'punishment' would have
been considerably diminished if not completely obvlivated.

> The judge, of course, has discretion to rule on these things and
> may feel that outside conspiring to take retribution on a player
> for previous behaviour might constitute collusion.

It's clearly collusion. The judge has latitude about whether it
consititutes illegal collusion, i.e. "collusion to alter the
results of a game" (which is rather ambiguous in certain respects).
But I think it really has to in order to avoid a potentially very
bad situation and maintain the integrity of VEKN tournaments.

Fred

however, for seeing that he was about to be dealt off the table, making
a better offer, and then CRUSHING his opponents who forgot that it was a
card game, and were too trusting.

Plus, I build decks that can win. One of the questions you must answer
when building your deck is: What will I do if my prey leaves all his
minions untapped?

If your deck cannot answer that question, it is weak.
If its only answer is "make deals", it is weak.

Play like you got a pair, not like you've got to collude.

-- Derek

Messages.Author: Orpheus
Messages.Body:
> "Orpheus" <orphe...@DEADSPAM.free.fr> writes:
>
> > NEVER !! There is absolutely no valid reason for that. And read LSJ'
lips :
> > "There are no rules for deals". Which is part of the problem (there
should
> > be rules *against* deals). But you cannot be forced to respect something
> > which doesn't exist, right ?
>
> If we assume that that premise is true (which I'm not commenting on
> for now), how would you propose to rule against deals?

I and some other people have already made several proposals in this thread.
Maybe you didn't have to time to read them yet.

> As LSJ pointed out recently, there are many different kinds of deals
> and the ones which seem to cause most problems are the ones that are
> perceived as spoiling other people's "fun, or somesuch".

As far as I'm concerned, the only deals that make me throw up are the deals
for VPs, because of their "final" aspect (if respected, which seems very
important to some people). I have no trouble whatsoever with temporary
deals, which always give you the possibility to change your mind and always
the necessity to optimize your VPs.

> Additionally, it's intrinsic to some facets of the game - politics
> particularly - that deals of some kind will have to be struck. If I
> don't split my KRC three to my prey and one to your prey (perhaps, on
> a five player table, you're my grand-prey and he's my grand-predator),
> you're going to vote it down, particularly if you're suspecting that
> (say) I'm going to Cryptic Rider it. At least you get something out
> of it this way.

See above. It would be stupid to take away this great part of the game,
which may be the single reason why it is the greatest of all CCGs.

> I'll leave to one side the problem of situations where I do sacrifice
> something short term, but for a similarly short term gain e.g. I'll
> pass that KRC for you, even though it does hurt me a bit now, but it
> lines me up for a kill on my prey. Or even "Okay, I'll give you those
> votes." But... it's worth bearing in mind that some of these can be
> seen as deals, and if you want to draw a line between a "deal" and
> cross-table negotiation, you're going to need to start drawing general
> principles for some judgement-oriented help. Where does that line get
> drawn?

To where people start not optimizing, even if they have already won the GW ;
or where two or more players collide "legally" to ruin the game for all the
others towards a predestined ending ; or where people start discarding cards
without playing them, or not playing the game and waiting for time limit. In
other words : I want to play this game, not a silly caricature of it.

> So, as two political decks, we're going to need to have some sort of
> long term negotiations. Now, you could say that a good player would
> be including Closed Session (or similar) - but that's not necessarily
> the point. Perfectly reasonable situations can occur where two people
> are, in fact, playing largely contradictory styles. Say, we're both
> playing a 1/2 Ventrue Law Firm. We may well need to co-operate over
> votes, we may well need to co-operate over who brings out which
> vampires. "Hey, is that Arika? She's got nine blood on her. It's
> just I have two vamps here, and one's Queen Anne and the other's Arika
> and I don't want to contest or waste my transfers."
>
> Of course, the other VLF player can lie through their teeth and try
> and screw me over (or feign innocence - the "Bugger, I've been
> transferring to the wrong vampire" face is worth practising). But if
> he doesn't - and he's possibly of the opinion that working together
> where it's mutually beneficial is better than clash of the titans -
> then we have a long term negotiating point going on.
>
>
> The point of all this setup is... Is that a deal that spoils other
> people's fun, or is that a deal which doesn't, or is it a deal in the
> first place? After all, repeated negotiation may *not* be a deal.
>
> (The above strikes me as good play, totally valid. But that's just my
> opinion.)

It is mine also. Under the condition that no table split is made. Then, when
and if it comes to that, those two players will clash anyway and one will
remain once the dust settles. Two political decks uniting, players avoiding
contest, players agreeing to get the Malk out of the table, voters /
bleeders getting rid of the rusher, all that is perfectly valid game :
because it is acting temporarily together for a common goal. Anyone can and
will change its mind at any time, and, more important, the game remains
suspenseful and everyone can keep on playing to the best of his ability.

> Would it make any difference if the two of us were playing, say,
> Euro-ish-Brujah and I negotiated to bring out Donal and Anvil, and you
> to bring out Constanza and Volker?

No.

(snip lots of precise examples of non-table-splitting deals)

> So where can you rule against these "deals" in general?

I think by now you understand what I mean. If you wish more precisions, feel
free to ask.

> > Good players don't need deals to do what they must.
> >
> > Bad players don't need deals to screw a table.
>
> I think these are both invalid premises, in that they're generalised
> principles which fail to take into account individual situations.
>
> I'm on a table playing, say, a Baltimore Purge deck. Eat vampires,
> destroy them. Now, this is going to incur the wrath of the whole
> table most likely (save for a few ally decks, but leave that out of it
> - it's very unlikely, but it's still a remote possibility). So you
> could say that as a "good" player, I shouldn't have played that deck.

BP decks are, I know from experience, very hard to play : getting the win
and not just screwing the table requires careful setting and good play.

You'll notice I said nothing about incurring table wrath being a proof of a
bad deck. Risky, but it can sometimes be worth it.

> But, move on to a far more innocuous deck. It just happens that it's
> the antithesis of my predator and prey - for a casual example, let's
> say I'm playing a very fast combat deck, and they can't deal with it
> at all. So they need to get me ousted. First, is that a deal from
> their point of view? As the prey, I really, really, really don't care
> that my grand-predator gets a VP out of this - I need that deck off
> the table, RIGHT NOW.

Agreed. As I said, it's perfectly valid play : both player will get somthing
out of this. Dealing with each other will wait until then. Now, if there was
a deal for VPs at this point, we'd get on to a planned and annoying game.
OTOH, I would find it normal to ask of the future predator a few turns a
respite, or some kind of payback ; of course nothing prevents him from not
accepting or not keeping his word.

> Here, we can't really say that it's my fault per se. As a good
> player, I just happened to have picked a deck and two average players
> (though their skill doesn't necessarily come into it) happen to have
> decks that are very vulnerable to it. So two players really need me
> off the table.

Agreed. (snip more examples towards same end ; sorry, I just don't have the
time, and I don't think it's necessary to explain these specific examples as
you now have a more precise idea of my real thoughts on the matter).

> > But deals certainly encourage making wrong decisions and ruining some
games
> > for one meager VP.
>
> It can. But what about the situations where the *right* decision is
> to go with that deal? How do you propose to stop people winning
> through good play?

I don't know if we're talking table-splitting here. I'll never want to stop
people from playing well !! But I want them to play to the end.

> > Deals for 1 VP should never exist : the deck making the "winning deal"
> > should be able to win without the deal (if not, it would be illegal,
right
> > ?) ; the deck making the "losing deal" should just die painfully and
not
> > take the other players' potential for VPs away.
>
> No, this isn't true in either respect. (There may be some situations
> where it is - probably lots - but it's not universally true.)
>
> The classic example of this has often been two hard combat decks
> sitting next to each other.

As a matter of fact, it is the classical "only" example where deals seem
totally necessary. Well, let me tell you that as a judge I ruled against a
splitting deal in just such a situation. The players wanted to deal VPs in
the first 15 minutes of the game. I ruled against it again later in the
game. And I was proved right : they played well with temporary deals, and at
one point one was able to sweep (but didn't because he had promised one turn
of respite) and later on it was the other that won (although the second
combat deck finally made 0). How did they achieve that ? By careful and
intelligent play rather than predetermining the issue of the table in the
first rounds of the game, which would have been boring for everyone. So :
deals are not always a fatality.

> (Indeed, this was one of the situations
> that brought about the Table Win rulings, based on much bitching about
> such situations. The TW rule provides incentives for both of the
> combat decks to want to be on the 4 side of that deal, however, which
> may make the deal harder to broker.)

Sometimes they will have to work together towards that goal. No need to
split the table.

Also, shit can happen (anti-deck etc) where you won't make a single VP
without deal, but then that, as you pointed earlier, can happen to any deck.
There are of course safeguards : you may, depending on your deck, include
ways to change places, to immobilize or burn a vampire, a few stealth cards
in a fight deck (Swallowed for Assamites), etc. Good players always include
a Plan B. Great players can include a Plan C and sometimes D without
de-optimizing their decks.

> I have a combat deck, you (my prey) also have a combat deck. I need
> to bleed through you, and to do that, I want to destroy your vampires.
> (There's nothing wrong so far, this is classic rush deck stuff.)
>
> However, to destroy your vampires, I need to go into combat. You can
> hit back. You probably will hit back.
>
> Now, assuming that we're both playing a combat deck that's largely
> offense with only a little defence, it could work out that we'll
> mutually annihilate each other. (The canny Gangrel fortitude player
> may be in a very different situation, of course.) Say, it's two (very
> different) Brujah combat decks that are going to destroy each other.
> You're playing Euro-Brujah mostly, I'm doing something fun with Group
> 3, say. Or Brujah vs Tzimisce - we both have a little damage
> prevention/avoidance floating around (e.g. Sideslip, various little
> bits of Vicissitude), but we're both conscious that the deck probably
> doesn't have a whole lot.
>
> However, the specific example doesn't matter too much - we can both
> find situations where combat decks next to each other will annihilate
> each other.

Agreed, of course.

> Now, if they're the last two decks on the table, it's
> likely that one will last a little longer than the other and find
> itself able to bleed out the other player with a copy of Hasina Kesi
> over multiple turns and a well-timed copy of Fame.

LOL.

> But on a five player table, both of us will probably die and my
> predator will destroy me, then you. 0 VPs each. And you probably
> can't get a single VP because I'm killing your vampires.
>
> So, we're both in a situation of 0 VP. (This can happen.)

Yes. OR : you could agree to get soft for a while, and both build up.
Depending on your decks, you'll each go your way, or pool, or whatever.
Then, with play, some strange situations may arise : like one where you prey
has tapped all of his vampires and has no way to Wake, or he has exhausted
the Combat cards you were so afraid of against other players, or some cards
go round and your way (Anarch Troublemaker ?) or a Vote deck changes places,
or someone proposes an alliance (you'll notice I spoke of no deal here) to
you towards a mutual goal, etc. This game is never frozen, especially with
good players, and that's what I love so much about it.

> If I can convince you to take the deal whereby you oust your prey,
> then I sweep the table, I'm playing for a TW. You can't get a TW, so
> the deal still allows you to maximise your VPs. (Of course, someone
> else might be able to offer you a *better* deal - but you're not
> obliged to take it, if you think they're lying etc.)
>
> So, from 0 VPs you get 1 VP. From 0 VPs, I get a TW and 4 VPs.
>
> Classically, it gets split 3-2 (you get the rest of the table and roll
> over for me to get my pound of flesh), but various reasons might
> convince you to take my deal, which is still an improvement on 0.
>
> You don't have to take the deal, but if we allow that we're both
> pretty sure we're going to kill each other (small tournament, played
> each other before, single table tournament etc.) which is far from
> impossible with two meaty combat decks, the deal isn't illegal.

Sure. But there can still be other ways. Say you both begin to destroy the
table : some other players at some point may propose other solutions to you.
Now, if you've already dealt for VPs, and, say, you want to keep your word,
this possibility is over and the game is boring ; if you just agreed on some
turn-after-turn strategies, you can trade alliances without even "breaking"
your word.

> And - as above - you try explaining to the player that he can't get a
> TW that way, and has to get 0 VP instead, even though an in-game,
> non-collusive piece of play allows him to do so without requiring
> another player to worsen their expected outcome based on the table at
> hand.

Working for a while towards a common goal can be acceptable.

Determining the fate of the table isn't.

Welcome back,

Orpheus

> > Forcing people to break the deal if they suddenly get a chance to
> > actually win the game, would drastically lower the sick vp deals...
>
> You cannot force a player to make a deal, you cannot force him to
> break it. Sorry to say it, but its an absurd proposition.

Not absurd at all. The rule wouldnt be about forcing people to break
deals. It would be about forcing people to ALWAYS play for more VP's,
which is pretty simple.
If someone have ousted their prey and then stops doing anything and
transfers down to 1 pool while not blocknig any of his predators
bleeds, I would say it was pretty obvious that he wasnt trying to
maximize his VP's.

>
> > Example: In a 3 player end game i let my prey kill my predator. If he
> > still has no chance of ousting me he should off course be allowed to
> > honor the deal and kill himself, since it wont make a difference..
> > only a matter of time.
> > BUT if the 6 pool and other circumstances makes it possible for him to
> > oust me now, he should be forced to do so by the rules.
>
> Rules that cannot be forced, should not exist.

Please explain what part of the "If you have any chance of getting
more VP's you must try to do so, even if it means breaking a former
deal" rule that you think is impossible to enforce?

Nikolaj Wendt
