Messages.Author: James Coupe
Messages.Body:
"Orpheus" <orphe...@DEADSPAM.free.fr> writes:

Missing attribution line for my text. :( Most newsreaders include
these by default to make a conversation easier to follow.

> > "Orpheus" <orphe...@DEADSPAM.free.fr> writes:
> >
> > > NEVER !! There is absolutely no valid reason for that. And read LSJ'
> lips :
> > > "There are no rules for deals". Which is part of the problem (there
> should
> > > be rules *against* deals). But you cannot be forced to respect something
> > > which doesn't exist, right ?
> >
> > If we assume that that premise is true (which I'm not commenting on
> > for now), how would you propose to rule against deals?
>
> I and some other people have already made several proposals in this thread.
> Maybe you didn't have to time to read them yet.

I have. I think they're misguided. Hence my post.

The problem is not the proposition of "We want to ban this, this and
this". The problem is whether you understand what such a proposal
involves, and what the reality of implementing such things is. I
would humbly submit that you haven't thought through what it means in
reality, nor how you would actually enforce such a proposal.

It is all too tempting to think "Well, we have these VP split deals in
my group/my tourneys/my area, and we all know what we mean and we want
them banned."

This can work fine as a social obligation, since "everyone" knows what
it is - in as much as any social obligation of that sort ever will.
See Derek Ray's (and other people's) posts on the problem of enforcing
things socially. There have been posts about it through the ages,
there's no need to go over it all again. Essentially, social
obligations of that sort are bad for the game. You have unwritten
rules or unwritten/imprecise understandings that prevent new players
understanding what on earth you're doing.

But if these unwritten understandings and friendly agreements were so
all pervasive, we wouldn't have buckets of rules, rulings,
clarifications and so forth rolling round. Everyone would just "know"
what the rules were, wouldn't they? After all, bear in mind Richard
Garfield pointed out that one reading of the text "You lose next turn"
by a player was "The opponent loses the game next turn" as opposed to
"You skip your next turn". (It's in one of the Magic books - intro to
the annotated fourth edition, I think, since that's the last one I
read before I had to talk to someone about such things.)

People play to win. And people want to know what they can do and what
they can't do before they start. People often play to find
"loopholes" - not actual loopholes, but being able to push the rules
as far as they can go, creating new interactions and the like. The
same is true of any other situation.

You need to be able to tell players what a "VP deal" entails, if
you're going to ban them. You haven't.

> > As LSJ pointed out recently, there are many different kinds of deals
> > and the ones which seem to cause most problems are the ones that are
> > perceived as spoiling other people's "fun, or somesuch".
>
> As far as I'm concerned, the only deals that make me throw up are the deals
> for VPs, because of their "final" aspect (if respected, which seems very
> important to some people). I have no trouble whatsoever with temporary
> deals, which always give you the possibility to change your mind and always
> the necessity to optimize your VPs.

So you have a problem.

You have a *big* problem.

What you have entirely failed to take into account is that what you're
saying is that all people have to do is mention the VPs people can get
out of a long term deal and, boom, you want to nuke their deal.

There's a reason I picked some quite elaborate, realistic examples.

Add to each of them an out-in-the-open consideration of "And that'll
net you two VPs and me three VPs instead of us stalling each other
completely" and the deal has suddenly switched from something you
admit is perfectly legitimate to something you believe is the spawn of
Satan.

If adding a thirty second explanation to the end of a deal explaining
how the table can/will fall to try and convince someone to take it
renders it illegal, I think you have a major, MAJOR problem in your
line of thinking.

Which would you rather have? Players able to actually be honest when
they want, or players who are forced to not actually say "Oh, and
that'll get you two VPs and me three VPs" out of it? The difference
is entirely in the fact that it's now out in the open. The table deal
is still exactly the same. The effect is still exactly the same.

Why the lack of objection to slicing up the table when you don't
mention VP splits, but a major objection to it when someone does?

> > Additionally, it's intrinsic to some facets of the game - politics
> > particularly - that deals of some kind will have to be struck. If I
> > don't split my KRC three to my prey and one to your prey (perhaps, on
> > a five player table, you're my grand-prey and he's my grand-predator),
> > you're going to vote it down, particularly if you're suspecting that
> > (say) I'm going to Cryptic Rider it. At least you get something out
> > of it this way.
>
> See above. It would be stupid to take away this great part of the game,
> which may be the single reason why it is the greatest of all CCGs.

But... as we all know, two political decks (by which I mean focused
political decks, as opposed to say a vote/Archon combat deck, where
the emphasis is different) can easily stall each other.

You need to get VPs, I need to get VPs. Unless one of us can take an
early lead, it's going to be very resource intensive if we fight it
out - I need to blow Awe and Bewitching Oration on every vote, you
need to do similar (using whatever method of vote push you have
available). So we make a deal to aid each other. The result of that
is to make it easy for me to kill my prey/your predator (same player),
and you probably get an okay ride at your prey (my grand-predator)
since I can probably convince you to throw some of your KRC points at
my prey too, so he goes a bit more quickly.

And if I explain this, and explain what VPs we're both hoping to get,
does this deal become illegal? We've decided how we're slicing the table.

If it does, you have a problem.

If it doesn't, why isn't it a forbidden VP deal? We're dealing to
split the table in a fashion whereby we allocate who gets what VPs.
We're deciding how it will happen, which of us will get the TW (we
hope).

It certainly smells like a VP deal from here. But if it isn't - which
it might not be, we don't have a sensible definition yet - you still
have the huge problem that it both looks and smells like a deal which
trades VPs for assistance.

> > I'll leave to one side the problem of situations where I do
> > sacrifice something short term, but for a similarly short term
> > gain e.g. I'll pass that KRC for you, even though it does hurt me
> > a bit now, but it lines me up for a kill on my prey. Or even
> > "Okay, I'll give you those votes." But... it's worth bearing in
> > mind that some of these can be seen as deals, and if you want to
> > draw a line between a "deal" and cross-table negotiation, you're
> > going to need to start drawing general principles for some
> > judgement-oriented help. Where does that line get drawn?
>
> To where people start not optimizing, even if they have already won the GW ;

Reasonably implausible.

What does "optimising" mean? We can't stop bad play. People can and
do play badly. The judge cannot step in and say "Take the pool for
the edge, dummy" or "But you have Jake Washington you can block with!"
or "If you'd done this and this, you could've got that VP on your
own."

Similarly, people also often get into situations where they could
probably get the TW with your aid, but might, maybe, possibly get the
TW on their own if they don't. Now, *you* might be able to get that
TW on your own, you might be a better player. But he's not as good a
player. It might have many, many moving parts. I might get confused,
lost or not understand one of the finer points of something I can do,
even though it's legally possible.

Now, this is the best move *for me* because I'll probably screw up the
other version.

How am I not optimising here? I've got the GW both ways. One way
involved me giving someone else two VP which needn't have happened.
Not all players *can* optimise, though.

We have all, I think, stood behind someone and thought "For Christ's
sake, just get on with it and stop trying to do things which are too
clever." (I've certainly posted about such things in the past.) I
have several times felt that a player would be optimising by getting
some VP now, because their deck is too fragile to try the table sweep
they're trying to set up.

Who is optimising now? Now I feel that letting someone else get a VP
so that I can consolidate two for myself *right now* would be a much
better "optimisation" because there are too many balls ready to fall.

The "optimisation" here is to not play for all the VP. Perhaps I'm
wrong in my assessment. How would you propose I prevent players who
aren't optimising?

> or where two or more players collide "legally"

Assuming you mean "collude", collusion is never legal.

You would do well to not use the term "collusion" to mean "currently
legitimate deal making based on in-game considerations but where we
discuss TWs and VPs".

Collusion is entirely different! It involves out of game
determinations, typically pre-game organising that I let you win or
similar. This is nothing like making a deal based on the table at
hand.

Confusing "collusion" with "deal making" weakens your argument - it
makes it look like you don't understand the difference.

> to ruin the game for all the
> others towards a predestined ending ;

The political deck I describe does just that. It's trying to set up
negotiation for us so that we can both do well to the detriment of
others, because if we don't do well, we both die.

The combat deck does the same. By not pressuring you, I can generate
a better position for myself and for you.

Any sufficiently complex deal is aiming towards ruining the game for
all the others excluded from the deal. That's how you gain ground
over them.

In many ways, the *point of the game* is to ruin the game for all the
others towards a predestined ending - you winning. It's not written
that way in the rulebook, but the point is that you want to win.

> or where people start discarding cards without playing them, or not
> playing the game and waiting for time limit.

This can be a problem. However, if you have a time limit (which we
do, and need) and you have things which can happen (e.g. withdrawal)
which can benefit players, it's the sort of thing that can and will
happen.

There are several ways of addressing this. It is rarely the case that
arbitrary rulings banning such things are a good way forward. If
withdrawal during the rest of the game gives you a VP, an arbitrary
ruling that says that - even though it's in all your interests - you
can't do it now is nonsensical.

You are, again, sitting down with players and saying:

- This is in your interests.
- This is the way you can get the most out of this round.
- You can't do it.

A more useful tack - if such is a problem - is to provide a series of
disincentives. For instance, it might be worth considering the
implications of withdrawal not being worth a full VP. For instance,
were it worth only half a VP, there would be no difference between it
and timing out. In such an instance, it would be worth playing to the
end in case you could oust someone, since withdrawing now would gain
you nothing over timing out at the end. (Unless one of the people
likely to die is you. But if you're that precarious, the other people
on the table may have something to say about allowing you to withdraw
instead.)

Of course, there are several knock-on effects so such a proposal might
not be perfect.

Alternative proposals might be to, say, have any ties resolved by
withdrawls counting after non-withdrawals. So if you have 1 TW, 9 VPs
(a sweep and two twos) and I have a 1 TW, 9 VPs (a sweep and two twos)
*but* in one of my games I withdrew to get the two VP and we're tied
for last place into the finals (small tournament)... I lose, you get in.

This then makes more aggressive gains of VPs count "better" than
withdrawals. You then don't have to ban the deal itself. A
withdrawal is an inherently worse way to gain a VP than a
non-withdrawal/oust, then.

Alternatively again, you might want to look at the withdrawal rule
itself. If you decide you wanted to keep it (which you might not),
you might want to change it. Picking a random idea from my Big Hat Of
Random Ideas, only the first player to withdraw from a game receives a
VP. Someone who has a legitimate need to get the hell out of the game
can get a VP that way. But then it is *never* in the table's
interests to mutually withdraw.

Again, this is not perfect. (Though a couple of them have a certain
sense of... something to them. I admit it's three in the morning,
though.) But what isn't it?

It's not telling players "These are the facts of the game, in-game.
This is how you would get the best out of the game. But you can't do
it."

Telling players that you, as the judge, have to deliberately curtail
the best play is inherently wrong.

If the "best play" is wrong for some reason, fix that.

> In other words : I want
> to play this game, not a silly caricature of it.

Why is it a silly caricature to find the best course of action
(co-operating with that guy over there), discuss it, come up with a
mutually beneficial way for us to play the game and go ahead with it?

The point of the game is to win, right? And if you can't win, do the
best you can.

That's what I'm doing.

As it happens, this means that you don't win.

It is *completely designed* into the game that social factors are
important. People are supposed to be able to do things like oust
someone cross-table if they're being troublesome to them. As Garfield
explains, you don't get the VP and/or pool for that because you got
something else out of it. Destroying a troublesome predator might be
that reason. Getting help from someone else towards a goal of you own
might be it.

A game set in the World of Darkness's Jyhad which details
Machiavellian plots of treachery, backstabbing and trying to come out
on top is going to necessitate these factors. People are *supposed*
to deal with each other.

Now, where deals are not entirely illegal (that is, they are based on
out of game considerations and so forth, as defined under the
collusion penalties, or similarly under the play to win rules),
players are allowed to make them.

Some players might be bad at making them. Others might be very good
at making them. Similarly, some players can be good or bad at deck
construction. Others might be good at gauging probabilities and card
flow. Others might be good at having an amazing poker face and
working the table that way.

But social interaction and deal making is an inherent part of the game.

If it's a problem in a given game, there are several ways of dealing
with it:

- have a sufficiently impervious deck that you can push through it.
For instance, stealth and bleed can be remarkably resilient to being
ganged up on. Someone gangs up on you, you curl yourself up in a
bunker and do what you can fast.

- have a significant threat. This might not be the same as above, but
is sort of the next step down. Okay, I may not be able to win, but
I can certainly make sure you don't. That's a *very* significant
threat. You make that deal, I am going to make sure you die. This
is perfectly legal play by the way. If you're going to die with
zero VP, you can die in any manner you choose, right? My manner of
play is that I don't give two hoots about my "honour" of
making/breaking deals. But I want the same reputation system to
work in my favour. Make a deal to cut me off the table? I'm going
to do my best to obliterate you. Sure, two against one will kill
me. But you'll know that I'll do everything I can to destroy you.
Are you now having second thoughts about going through with it?
Maybe you should be. It might not be the case, but if I'm going to
cause that much trouble for you, is it going to be worth it? If
you're my predator trying to get rid of me, it's going to give my
prey an easy ride, say. Much harder to deal with him next...

- fight fire with fire. People play combat, you play combat defence.
People play bleed, you play bleed defence. Right? If people start
playing alliances, do the same thing yourself. Get him before he
gets you. Get the other players to help you just force them off the
table. Point out that two people co-operating like that is going to
kill them, too. Have sufficient things in your deck that you can
offer some flexibility into the deck. Being able to, say, Parity
Shift some pool to someone else is a good bargaining tactic. Or
Consanguineous Boon. Things which aren't just devoted to being
totally efficient to your deck. Give yourself something to do which
is going to mean you can fight off alliances. You'd include bleed
defence if you were scared of being screwed over by bleeds. Include
some alliance defence the same way. The threat of being able to
destroy someone, regardlesss of your own well-being, is a very
specialised form of this.

But sometimes, if someone out-maneuvers you on the table manipulation
side of the game, you will die. But being able to manipulate the
table is just as much a part of the game as being able to bleed. It's
how the game was designed. Just like you need to improve your
deck-building ability if you're not very good at that, if someone else
is good at manipulating the table against you, you need to get better
at dealing with that.

> > The point of all this setup is... Is that a deal that spoils other
> > people's fun, or is that a deal which doesn't, or is it a deal in the
> > first place? After all, repeated negotiation may *not* be a deal.
> >
> > (The above strikes me as good play, totally valid. But that's just my
> > opinion.)
>
> It is mine also. Under the condition that no table split is made.

Then you're just legislating about words. And words can be changed.

All I have to do is point out what's in my interests, what's in your
interests, and how the game might go. And we haven't made a table
split. We've just discussed some possibilities. Which any player can
see as an invitation to go along with it.

But then you need to prevent people ever discussing possible
strategies and how the game might go. And that really is necessary to
the game. I might need to be able to explain to a newbie what the
long term implications of a move might be. Not only will they learn
that way, but they could also make a major change to the game.

Similarly, if you start banning people from being frank and open about
what they really mean, this hurts several people. Non-natives to a
culture, for instance - the nuance of subtlety, sarcasm, innuendo and
body language, for instance, can vary a lot when you're not a native
speaker. Also, pick anyone with Asperger's Syndrome, for instance,
who are often very bad at picking up what other people are thinking
and feeling. If you could just discuss the details, none of this
would need to be a problem.

> Then, when
> and if it comes to that, those two players will clash anyway and one will
> remain once the dust settles.

Sure. So I just don't say. End-game scenarios, their likelihoods and
how difficult they'll be are discussed, not split deals.

Split deals benefit both the players involved. They are the best form
of play for the players. They are going to end up needing to do them,
whether they can legally discuss them or not. It means we both do
better than we would otherwise. That's all that matters.

It works for me, it works for the guy I'm dealing with. If that's the
case - which in legal VP deals, it is, necessarily so - we're going to
do it anyway.

> because it is acting temporarily together for a common goal. Anyone can and
> will change its mind at any time,

If that's the case, you have nothing to fear from VP split deals.

The end result is not determined. They can change their minds at any
time, after all.

> and, more important, the game remains
> suspenseful and everyone can keep on playing to the best of his ability.

As they can in a VP split deal.

The game has taken a very hostile turn against you. You can still
play to the best of your ability. Just like when you get complete
deck jam and all your bleed bounce has shuffled to the bottom. The
game is now very hostile for you. But you still play. You do
whatever you can to win.

It's no different when someone starts trying to deal against you. You
just need to play to the best of your ability. And if that isn't good
enough, the best players won - table manipulation is a skill in the
Jyhad, and you got out-played.

Hell, I get rings run around me by people being able to craft deals to
do this, that and the other. But I also have similar issues with
people building betters decks, or having better ideas. It doesn't
mean I try to ban those.

> > So where can you rule against these "deals" in general?
>
> I think by now you understand what I mean. If you wish more precisions, feel
> free to ask.

Sadly, I don't think you understand what you mean.

You're not thinking this through. You're trying to ban vague concepts
that you can't define. You're trying to use a ban to prevent the best
play for a player ensuing because you don't like that best play.

If the best play is inappropriate for the health of the game, it
shouldn't be the best play. But telling players "You cannot play to
the best of your ability, even though this would be the best thing for
you to do" will never work.

> > I think these are both invalid premises, in that they're generalised
> > principles which fail to take into account individual situations.
> >
> > I'm on a table playing, say, a Baltimore Purge deck. Eat vampires,
> > destroy them. Now, this is going to incur the wrath of the whole
> > table most likely (save for a few ally decks, but leave that out of it
> > - it's very unlikely, but it's still a remote possibility). So you
> > could say that as a "good" player, I shouldn't have played that deck.
>
> BP decks are, I know from experience, very hard to play : getting the win
> and not just screwing the table requires careful setting and good play.
>
> You'll notice I said nothing about incurring table wrath being a proof of a
> bad deck. Risky, but it can sometimes be worth it.

No, that's not a bad deck. Nor did I say it was.

However, the distinction I drew was that a "good player" who couldn't
handle the table wrath may have made an inappropriate choice. This is
nothing about the deck itself. The deck itself is a very good one,
potentially. I was hugely impressed last year by Beatrice During's
play of one. As I said at the time, I felt she over-extended herself
a couple of times when she should have gone for the early kill (see
the optimization section above). But some of the play was amazing,
both in choice of cards, table manipulation (the lack of wrath that
came her way was quite surprising) and some of the plays she made was
excellent to watch.

The point here is that a "good player" might pick a deck that they
can't handle. (Since this is a "good player", and not the best
possible player ever.) In that instance, it would be possibly be
their fault that they got table wrath.

Then they'd be in a situation of their own making. Provocative deck
combined with inability to handle it -> need for deal.

So here we can argue that they made a bad choice and that a truly good
player wouldn't have made that choice and so the good player wouldn't
need the deal. (This may turn out to be wrong, but the point is that
we're clearly dealing - in the next example - with a good player
making a good choice, as opposed to a good player making a potentially
questionable choice, as a Baltimore Purge deck could be, for
instance.)

> > But, move on to a far more innocuous deck. It just happens that it's
> > the antithesis of my predator and prey - for a casual example, let's
> > say I'm playing a very fast combat deck, and they can't deal with it
> > at all. So they need to get me ousted. First, is that a deal from
> > their point of view? As the prey, I really, really, really don't care
> > that my grand-predator gets a VP out of this - I need that deck off
> > the table, RIGHT NOW.
>
> Agreed. As I said, it's perfectly valid play

You said:

"Good players don't need deals to do what they must.

Bad players don't need deals to screw a table."

And then distinguish deals from "Deals for 1 VP should never exist".

As is common on Usenet, this part of my response was prefixed by the
relevant section to which I was responding.

You claimed that good players don't need deals to do what they must.
I disputed that.

Since the above is valid play, but the deal is necessary, your premise
that good players don't need deals to do what they must is wrong.

I need to survive. I need to offer a deal.

If I phrase the above as "Hi, James's predator, James is really,
really, really killing me. I can do X, Y and Z if you can do A, B or
C", apparently, you're okay with it. But I can also say things like
"... and you'll get the VP out of it, so will you help me out?" Or I
could say "And since you can't get through him on your own, it'll get
you 1 VP and he's the only worry on the table, so I'll get the rest I
think."

The end result is the same. The means by which we get there is the
same. It's a play I need to make, and it involves a deal which should
"never exist".

> : both player will get somthing
> out of this. Dealing with each other will wait until then. Now, if there was
> a deal for VPs at this point,

Voiced or unvoiced? Intelligent players will be able to see the VP
splitting available, even if no-one mentions it.

Do you - in your games - ever see that if you make that deal, you'll
be able to get a TW and he'll get a VP or two out of it (depending on
how fast you go)? It's far from impossible to see them. I keep
so-and-so in and fail that vote for you, it lines us up for X, Y and
Z. Boom. Same ending, same process. No-one mentioned VPs though.

> > It can. But what about the situations where the *right* decision is
> > to go with that deal? How do you propose to stop people winning
> > through good play?
>
> I don't know if we're talking table-splitting here. I'll never want to stop
> people from playing well !! But I want them to play to the end.

You haven't thought through your proposals.

Banning a VP split deal *is* stopping people from playing well. It
gives them the best outcome on the table. It's achievable through
viable, legal, in-game means (i.e. not collusion, unsportsmanlike and
so on).

You are actively proposing to have a judge intervene and stop people
from playing well, to the best of their abilities, you just haven't
realised this.

> > > Deals for 1 VP should never exist : the deck making the "winning deal"
> > > should be able to win without the deal (if not, it would be illegal,
> right
> > > ?) ; the deck making the "losing deal" should just die painfully and
> not
> > > take the other players' potential for VPs away.
> >
> > No, this isn't true in either respect. (There may be some situations
> > where it is - probably lots - but it's not universally true.)
> >
> > The classic example of this has often been two hard combat decks
> > sitting next to each other.
>
> As a matter of fact, it is the classical "only" example where deals seem
> totally necessary.

I don't think this is true.

Certainly, it is a very prominent example. However, a player can find
himself in very deep problems, but could be rescued by intervention
from someone else, to mutual benefit. If we're down to three people
(perhaps it was a four player table to start, perhaps it's an 11
playertournament), let's say it's you, me, LSJ. LSJ is about to walk
all over me. If the two of us combine forces, we can get rid of LSJ.
It may be the case that with some help from you, I can stall LSJ long
enough for you to oust him. But I really do need your help. Perhaps
I need a point or two of blood to bring out Beast and rush his key
vampire. Perhaps I need lots of things. I need your help, or you die
too.

However, the price for my help is that I request a VP split so that
you oust LSJ and you roll over.

You get 1 VP (which is better than the 0 VP you were going to get) and
I get 2 VP (which is better than the 0 VP I was going to get) - maybe
a TW, too.

You have just banned this deal, and are banning players from playing
as well as they can.

Of course, you could choose to backstab me if you wanted, and I'd be
aware of that possibility.

The classical combat deck predator/prey possibility is one of it being
in their interests *early* in the game, to prevent mutual
annihilation. In the above situation, being able to at least offer
the VP split deal is the only way I'm going to go through with it. I
don't want to help you out for no reason - all that means is I get to
let you win instead of LSJ, say. I can be Kingmaker. And in this
instance, if you want any slice of the pie, I want to make you give me
some too.

> Well, let me tell you that as a judge I ruled against a
> splitting deal in just such a situation. The players wanted to deal VPs in
> the first 15 minutes of the game. I ruled against it again later in the
> game. And I was proved right : they played well with temporary deals, and at
> one point one was able to sweep (but didn't because he had promised one turn
> of respite) and later on it was the other that won (although the second
> combat deck finally made 0).

There are two possible situations that spring to mind - there are
certainly other possibilities, too:

- This is quite possibily *not* the classical combat deck. The
problem that the classical deck generates is that I am a combat
deck. My prey is also a combat deck. For me to make forward
motion, I have to attack your vampires. I can't get rid of you
until they're gone. If I let you go round the table, I'll never get
through anyway as you get extra pool. But if I rush you, we both
implode. There isn't a short term deal we can make that's in my
interest. All the short-term interests in the world can't give me
anything I need. I NEED YOU DEAD. If this is the case, all you do
is tell people that if they just make things *sound* like short term
deals, they can make a long term VP split.

- This is not the classical combat deck situation for other reasons.
One or the other deck has an edge. Clearly, if one is sweeping,
there's something of an edge! The classical situation is that I
need to get through you, because you are my prey at the start of the
game. If I let you get up a head of steam, I die anyway! So I'm
going to try to kill you to get through you. If this situation does
happen but one can survive and sweep, it's not the classical mutual
annihilation situation, and hence isn't really an example of why the
classical situation doesn't work, because it's not that situation.

> How did they achieve that ? By careful and
> intelligent play rather than predetermining the issue of the table in the
> first rounds of the game, which would have been boring for everyone. So :
> deals are not always a fatality.

Sure, it could be boring. If you *let* them predetermine the table,
you deserve everything you get. There's three players, two others you
can ally with, on a five player table. Why are you letting them do this?

> > (Indeed, this was one of the situations
> > that brought about the Table Win rulings, based on much bitching about
> > such situations. The TW rule provides incentives for both of the
> > combat decks to want to be on the 4 side of that deal, however, which
> > may make the deal harder to broker.)
>
> Sometimes they will have to work together towards that goal. No need to
> split the table.

Then you're just quibbling about words. If we're next to each other
at the start, as in the classical example, I'm not going to help you
without some payback. If that payback can only come by you dying,
you're allowing people to do the same, you're just not letting them be
honest about it.

> Also, shit can happen (anti-deck etc) where you won't make a single VP
> without deal, but then that, as you pointed earlier, can happen to any deck.
> There are of course safeguards : you may, depending on your deck, include
> ways to change places, to immobilize or burn a vampire, a few stealth cards
> in a fight deck (Swallowed for Assamites), etc. Good players always include
> a Plan B. Great players can include a Plan C and sometimes D without
> de-optimizing their decks.

Toolbox decks, for instance, can do such things very well. And some
deck styles lend themselves very well to such things, by virtue of
using a lot of dual-type cards. e.g. Distraction, which has two very
different effects.

But there are many different deck styles, and individual personal
preferences about such deck styles aren't relevant.

People play focused decks, toolbox decks, bruise-and-bleed,
vote-and-bloat, ally decks and all sorts of decks.

If the argument is that "My rules on deals work well when played by
people I play with", you're missing the point. Your experiences of
such things are going to reflect your play-group and tourney
experience.

Additionally, if the two combat decks are being diverse and having
other alternatives, this does prove that the situation you're
describing isn't the classical predator/prey combat deck situation
where they have to destroy vampires to stand a chance.

> > But on a five player table, both of us will probably die and my
> > predator will destroy me, then you. 0 VPs each. And you probably
> > can't get a single VP because I'm killing your vampires.
> >
> > So, we're both in a situation of 0 VP. (This can happen.)
>
> Yes. OR : you could agree to get soft for a while, and both build up.

I don't want you to build up. It's not in my interests. You building
up means it's easier for you to get through your prey. Which gives
you more pool, which I can't get because I can't oust you, oh and a VP.

If you really are doing nothing, you've just given your prey an easy
ride too, which completely destabilises the table.

This is not in my interests.

> Depending on your decks, you'll each go your way,

My way involves KILLING ALL YOUR VAMPIRES. This is how it works. I
need you to die.

> or pool, or whatever.
> Then, with play, some strange situations may arise : like one where you prey
> has tapped all of his vampires and has no way to Wake,

Sure, people can do unthinkably stupid things.

However, you're playing a combat deck. Even allowing for Computer
Hacking, you typically can't do more than two pool damage. Oh, and
the only pool damage you've taken is that coming from me, largely.
Which is none, because I need your vampires to die. So you largely
have a lot of control over how much pool you have, based on how much
you've spent on vampires.

> or he has exhausted
> the Combat cards you were so afraid of against other players,

Only I can't particularly cycle *anything* to use against people, so
I'm lumped with a hand that isn't of my choosing. You've had the
ability to cycle through the cards you want, keep the cards you wanted
to keep in reserve. You know I'm on the table. Why would you be so
stupid as to leave yourself entirely vulnerable to me killing all your
vampires, save for deck-jam?

> or some cards
> go round and your way (Anarch Troublemaker ?) or a Vote deck changes places,
> or someone proposes an alliance (you'll notice I spoke of no deal here)

It amounts to the same thing. You just haven't mentioned it. I need
your help to get VPs and if you don't want my help to get you VPs, why
are you offering me anything? We're going to start slicing up
sections of the table, and ruining the fun of others into
predetermined fashions. You just think it's more fun if you're not
allowed to be honest about this.

> to
> you towards a mutual goal, etc.

The mutual goal of us destroying the rest of the table if we can? We
are playing towards that. That's the goal. We both need VPs.

> This game is never frozen, especially with
> good players, and that's what I love so much about it.

The rules aren't just made for "good players" using decks with Plans
A, B, C and D.

Changing the rules to fit your playgroup and expertise is not a good
idea.

> > If I can convince you to take the deal whereby you oust your prey,
> > then I sweep the table, I'm playing for a TW. You can't get a TW, so
> > the deal still allows you to maximise your VPs. (Of course, someone
> > else might be able to offer you a *better* deal - but you're not
> > obliged to take it, if you think they're lying etc.)
>

> Sure. But there can still be other ways. Say you both begin to destroy the
> table : some other players at some point may propose other solutions to you.

Sure, there are other possibilities.

The classical situation, however, is that I need to get through you,
so I need you dead. If someone else can't kill you right now, I'm
mostly screwed.

Additionally, it is a general truth that a loan combat deck on a table
is in a difficult position. Lots of people have a smattering of
combat defence. Two combat decks on a table can easily draw through
that, whereas one can run up against enough to stall it a little.

It's often not in a combat deck's interests to have the other combat
deck on the table off the table - it's just one of those really,
really frustrating sitautions when they end up sitting next to each
other at the start of the game. This is the crucial point.
Cross-table, fine. Sitting next to each other, I NEED YOU TO DIE IF I
WANT TO GET ANYWHERE. Like I said, once you get down to the last two
(one of us having one VP, the other having two), the two VPs can go
either way. But if I want anything when we sit next to each other, I
NEED YOU TO DIE.

> Now, if you've already dealt for VPs, and, say, you want to keep your word,

You don't have to keep your word. You might assume some people will.
But that's not a valid assumption on which to base all rules changes,
since plenty of other groups have realised that, when playing a game,
breaking your word can be advantageous.

So this isn't a valid assumption.

> this possibility is over and the game is boring

Why on earth are you assuming that VP splits mean that possibilities
are over? People can backstab. People do backstab.

Your group might not. But again, changes aren't made just on your
group.

> ; if you just agreed on some
> turn-after-turn strategies, you can trade alliances without even "breaking"
> your word.

Why be so pointlessly hung up on keeping your word? If the problem is
VP splits which can't be shaken because you won't do deals with the
rest of the table and no-one will break their word, this is becoming
sufficiently specific to a particular metagame that you're just never
going to change the game for that. Other people make VP splits,
backstab, ally, counter-ally, ignore deals and play with all sorts of
weirdness and it seems to work. Why change the rules because your
environment won't move beyond it?

> > And - as above - you try explaining to the player that he can't get a
> > TW that way, and has to get 0 VP instead, even though an in-game,
> > non-collusive piece of play allows him to do so without requiring
> > another player to worsen their expected outcome based on the table at
> > hand.
>
> Working for a while towards a common goal can be acceptable.
>
> Determining the fate of the table isn't.

The fate of the table hasn't been determined.

What they *want* the fate of the table to be has been determined.

By the way, this was already determined when you sat down at the
table. You wanted to sweep the table. All that's happened is that
that intended fate has changed.

Making a VP split deal doesn't set a table in stone. If you think it
does, it's your table that's the problem. The people who are winning
on the VP split deals are simply playing better than you, and you
haven't bested them yet. Deal making is part of the game. It's where
you're losing.

Have fun trying.

--
James Coupe

Messages.Author: Chris Shorb
Messages.Body:
Orpheus wrote:

> My question to LSJ and staff is very simple : do you plan to legifere the
> deals in any way (including forbidding them, or making a one-line rule, or a
> 20-pages notebook...) in the time to come ?

Finally read all the way through most of this thread, except for the
tremendously long posts by Coupe.

My suggestion is a simple one. There is already a rule against stalling. There
is no rule supporting deal-making. If the discussion of a deal is taking too
long, and it bothers you, make a stink, shut the deal makers up, and get the
play moving again. Easier said than done. But if done enough, then deal making
will revert back to the example LSJ gave. "I KRC" "Will I take damage?" "No"
"No block". A table split deal IME takes a long time to explicate and come to
terms.

Also, Legbiter/Josh's suggestion that breaking deals leads to better play also
dovetails in with Curevei's comments that deals are bad play; because deals
that aren't mutually beneficial should, by evolution of a play group, lead to
better play through cooperation that doesn't need a deal, or a deal with the
implicit assumption that at some point, it will be broken, at that moment when
it no longer is *mutually* beneficial.

To make a short story long, there already are mechanisms in place for deals -
collusion is illegal, stalling is illegal. Use either or both as a scalpel or a
cudgel to keep the pace of play moving, and the goals focused on winning through
smart card play, not the best talker.



Messages.Author: LSJ
Messages.Body:
Chris Shorb wrote:
> My suggestion is a simple one. There is already a rule against stalling. There
> is no rule supporting deal-making. If the discussion of a deal is taking too
> long, and it bothers you, make a stink, shut the deal makers up, and get the
> play moving again. Easier said than done. But if done enough, then deal making
> will revert back to the example LSJ gave. "I KRC" "Will I take damage?" "No"
> "No block". A table split deal IME takes a long time to explicate and come to
> terms.

If a deal-making discussion is viewed (by the judge) as "attempting to
stall to take advantage of a time limit", then she should step in (and,
in all likelyhood, simply add back the time that was lost). But that remedy
won't prevent deals from being made. The judge cannot masquerade behind the
stalling rule to undermine legal play that she finds distasteful.

Messages.Author: Daneel
Messages.Body:
> And, he's bragging about his unsportsmanlike behavior. Screwing one of
> your friends in a later game to "punish" him for breaking a deal, even
> if you weren't the one hurt by the dealbreak,... that's just weak, and
> it's lame, and it's all bad.

Maybe the angle of "punishment" is poor. Try "illustration". Showing the
other person what it is like to be backstabbed. In the given instance the
"retributor" may have gained an advantage from betrayal, even if the real
cause was to illustrate the down side to the formerly treacherous player.

> And he pretends that it is the best thing
> ever and should be enforced by the rules? Oh, hell no. Someone does
> that to me, I probably never play with that person again, EVER. It's
> one thing to backstab me in a game to gain a VP; it's another thing
> entirely to front-stab me in a LATER game and say "It is because of what
> you did last Tuesday!"... and then pretend you have some moral high
> ground. Plleeeeeeease.

In a game I once stole an AR from my prey's Fatima with one of my
!Torries. By twist of fate, I had the same guy at my next table, only in a
cross-table position. When I blocked his deflected bleed with my !Torrie
who had a Bang Nakh, he stole it (and told me we were now "quits"). Took
me a while to figure what he meant... ;) I couldn't really understand his
motives. Specifics about games should not be remembered (but general
conclusions may - in this case, I noted for further reference that the
person can be erratic in his behaviour).

> Let's get perspective, folks. It's a game in a gothic, dark setting,
> about ancient vampires, intrigue, treachery, and betrayal. It is NOT a
> suitable game for those who must be Pillars of Honour(tm).

Words. A game about ancient vampires, yet we do not indulge in real blood
drinking, nor do we actually kill people. It is about intrigue, but that
does not mean we have to lie playing it. I would advise against taking the
role too seriously (lest we arrive at the "I roll a d4 to see whom I bleed
'cause I'm a MALKAVIAN and MALKAVIANS are kray-Z and kewl!" issue).

My take - I am a guy who sits down to play with a bunch of other guys. The
game has a theme, yes, but we are the same guys nevertheless. If you lie
to me "...because of this...", I will be inclined to assume that you are
not above lying to me "...because of that...". Same with betrayal. For me
this game is more about having the wits to win - or the guts to lose -
with dignity. Twisting words can be fun, but outright lies are lame and
not stylish enough for the theme. (Remember, we are the _players_.)

> And finally, we can look at Succubus Club: "...None are enforced by the
> rules." How much more clear can you be? Deal-breaking is encouraged.

Strawman. The reminder text on Succubus Club reminds you that the card
cannot enforce any additional terms. Thinking it over, it is obvious why.
I would not equate the statement reminding you of the unenforcability of
some terms of the deal with a hypothetical encouragement of breaking all
non-enforced parts of said deal...

--
Bye,

Daneel

Messages.Author: James Coupe
Messages.Body:
"Orpheus" <orphe...@DEADSPAM.free.fr> writes:

> I'm with you guys on this one. Nor do I think we're alone.
> If there are really no rules / rulings about deals, there is absolutely no
> problem whatsoever, and people will know that a deal that isn't anymore
> mutually beneficial will be broken.

If a deal is set-up such that the player is required to backstab the
moment the deal becomes detrimental to him, no player will ever "go
first" in a deal and therefore such deals cannot be made in the first
place. This would prevent the game from generating subtly crafted
deals of depth and intrigue. (There are many posts on Google about
this, over time.)

Whilst it would be difficult to rule in a case of minor dealing over
little bits of play of minor consequence, a general principle of "You
must break a deal if it's in your interest" would apply to those too.

Or is there some threshold over which a deal of that sort would be
measured and things under the radar need not be examined? Would you
care to define the general principle of when a player can keep a deal,
even though they might be able to do something better with that minion
(e.g. oust their prey instead of rescuing your vampire from torpor),
and when they can't?

Messages.Body:
"Reyda" <true_...@hotmail.com> writes:

> "Frederick Scott" <dont...@mymail.com> a écrit dans le message de
> news:Api7d.4002$mS1.813@fed1read05...

> > It's clearly collusion. The judge has latitude about whether it
> > consititutes illegal collusion, i.e. "collusion to alter the
> > results of a game" (which is rather ambiguous in certain respects).
> > But I think it really has to in order to avoid a potentially very
> > bad situation and maintain the integrity of VEKN tournaments.
>
> you know... i don't think it's collusion.

As I've said, it's aruably collusion - but possibly not.

However, I'm unsure where Frederick has got the idea that I'd have to
rule it collusion to maintain the integrity of a tournament. I've
already pointed out one way of dealing with it without requiring it to
be ruled as collusion - declaring it invalid under the Unsportsmanlike
rules, for a start.

>I go to a tournament, and someone at my table agrees to a deal with someone
>else and then "betrays".
>And later in this tournament, i meet him again and he tries to propose me a
>deal... What should i do then ? refuse knowing there will be some betrayal
>at some point ?

Well, for a start, you don't *know* that. People do funny things all
the time.

People can, have and very probably will back out on deals with me,
apologise for doing so but as we can both see, I'm going to do anyway
so there's nothing they can do to help. Or turn round and backstab me
in order to get a TW. Or whatever.

However, that doesn't happen all the time.

People don't just fall into categories of "deal honourer" and "deal
breaker". You can - very easily - find a player who'll backstab when
it's vitally important to them (they're about to be ousted, you're
going to die, they get a better offer which will probably get them the
TW or whatever) but not the rest of the time.

You are, of course, allowed to refuse the deal. You can even explain
why you're going to refuse the deal. You are never, ever required to
make a deal by the rules. Nor are you ever required to keep a deal,
by the rules. Nor are you required to play without a memory.

As people have repeatedly pointed out, "honour" as a virtue in some
players - that of keeping deals - is something they play with and
remember. Will Reyda keep the deal? Hmm... probably he will, I
think. So I'll take it over that one from the nasty Legbiter chap.
The reverse is similarly true - he breaks his deals, so I don't have

to go through with it.

A canny player might choose to take the deal and break it later, to
their advantage. (Assuming they're wily enough to do so.) For
instance, he agrees to "lend" you The Rack in order to generate some
blood, so you can push a vote with Awe, say. Except you don't give it
back. Many better examples could no doubt be concocted.

However, singling out a player based on out of game considerations
("He broke a deal in the last game", "He slept with my wife", "He's
black and I'm racist") rather than in-game considerations ("He's about
to oust me", "His deck is killing my ability to play" etc.) would be,
in many people's view I'd hazard, "wrong" even if not written
explicitly in the rules.

As I've said, I'd view such attacks as potential Unsportsmanlike
Conduct.

All of which is very different to whether or not you choose to deal
with a "deal breaker".



Yea, I get what you're saying. No, of course you can't. Agreed -
as I posted elsewhere - this kind of thing is unavoidable. But...

> I don't really understand your logic here. I don't see why Vekn
> players loose their integrity if they use some Zorro-type
> sentences to seal their acts.

I don't know what "Zorro-type sentence" is. But my logic is that
there's a *difference* between not trusting a guy because he's
broken a previous deal with you and actively screwing him over in
a later game because you felt he screwed you over in a previous
game. I'm not defending this distinction on any real logical
grounds except that: 1) the difference between lack of trust and
active revenge is very distinct (in the former case you are using
past experience to increase your chances of winning the later game;
in the latter case you are actually *sacrificing* your chances of
winning a game by attempting to decrease another player's chances
of winning) albeit if the player doing it doesn't verbally say what
he's doing, you may have to read his mind to know; and 2) the former
shouldn't really harm the interests of tournament participation
and the latter may very do so.

Is that at least reasonably clear?

Fred

No one knows how a situation on the game table can evolve, and there are
often great surprises on what really happens a few turns after a given,
apparently "frozen" gamestate. But the deals would certainly be more
cautious, yes.

> This would prevent the game from generating subtly crafted
> deals of depth and intrigue. (There are many posts on
> Google about
> this, over time.)

Then there is no need to discuss it again ?

Still, I disagree : the game can be just as subtle without table-split
deals. Keep in mind that this is what we're talking again here.

> Whilst it would be difficult to rule in a case of minor dealing over
> little bits of play of minor consequence, a general principle of "You
> must break a deal if it's in your interest" would apply to those too.

It may be in your interest to respect a small deal, and a judge has very few
means to evaluate that, nor does he has the right to tell a player how to
play.

But if deals look like collusion, or a non-optimisation of Vps, he can judge
and deal accordingly.

> Or is there some threshold over which a deal of that sort would be
> measured and things under the radar need not be examined? Would you
> care to define the general principle of when a player can keep a deal,
> even though they might be able to do something better with that minion
> (e.g. oust their prey instead of rescuing your vampire from torpor),
> and when they can't?

Now you pose something interesting. You know, for me the core of the problem
lies with table-splitting deals, formulated or suggested. You can, and often
do, make timing choices : it may be wiser not to kill your prey right away,
says, because you want her to weaken your next prey ; likewise, getting an
ally, however temporary, can be a wise thing : you help me, I help you ; I
keep my word, we may do it again (or not ; I may keep my word again ; or
not).

Such temporary deals do, as you say, add to the interests of this game (I
would have stopped some years ago without these subtleties).

You choose how, and in what timing, you will make those VPs. What counts is
: do as many as you possibly can !! If you don't : it's collusion.

Or bad play (I know a player who doesn't bleed to kill his prey and looses
games he should win ; just because he panics). But the judge should be able
to determine which one it is.

And all of us who had to judge deals know that the guidelines are just that,
and that ultimately it's the you, your logic and your conscience (there are
no rules about deals).

Hoping this will help you understand our viewpoint,



Messages.Author: Frederick Scott
Messages.Body:
"James Coupe" <ja...@zephyr.org.uk> wrote in message

> However, I'm unsure where Frederick has got the idea that I'd have
> to rule it collusion to maintain the integrity of a tournament.
> I've already pointed out one way of dealing with it without
> requiring it to be ruled as collusion - declaring it invalid under
> the Unsportsmanlike rules, for a start.

What? You're quibbling that players actually need to *collude*
in order to fall under "collusion"?!? How quaint! :-)

I guess the reasons I feel it belongs under "collusion" rather
than unsportsmanlike behavior is the "...to alter the results of
a game" part of collusion, which is what the offender is attempting
to do. I've always though of unsportsmanlike conduct as just that:
generally hostile behavior of an uncalled for nature. That is,
letting one's anger and frustration get out of control to where one
is screaming at opponents, judges, or others making the environment
generally unpleasant. But you can screw over an opponent with a
smile and a kind word on the side and that doesn't seem to fall
under unsportingmanlike behavior IME.

Also, I vaguely recall (read, "where my long-term memory is
concerned, all bets are off!" :-P ) LSJ generally grouping
anything involving outside acting on motivations that stem from
sources outside the game - including such things as feeling that
one needs only a single victory point to qualify for the finals
and so playing to get one sure VP instead of a game win - under
the collusion rule.

Bottom line, of course, is that I don't really care so much how
you enforce this situation as long as you do. If you want to call
"unsportsmanlike" instead of "collusion", I guess it's not that
important.

Fred

Messages.Author: Orpheus

> > Still, I disagree : the game can be just as subtle without table-split

It has never been my proposal to "mow down all deals". It would be rather
silly, limitating, not to mention impossible to define.

> If you want to limit it to just VP deals, then you need to
> phrase it that way (and come up with some way to define what
> is and what is not a "VP deal").

Okay, then let's try again : these are guidelines (I'll let the exact
phrasing to more expert rulers than me) that could be included in the rules
booklet without any further modification, and could "mow down" a lot of what
I consider "bad deals" (the ones that are bad for the spirit of the game,
meaning most of the VP deals) :

- modify ruling : a player must try to gain every possible VP at the table,
to the best of his ability (this does not stop at the Game Win)

- get rid of the Withdraw rule altogether (adapt text of Brinksmanship) ;
after all, I don't see why people who get to Time Limit should by mutual
agreement get 1 VP each instead of 0.5 : this was IMHO a loophole in the
rules, and has no valid reason of being kept. Even people without a library
can play, moreso at least than people without any ready vampire, and I don't
believe there's any rule allowing these to leave the table, is there ?
Withdrawing should allow no VP, or at the max 0.5, or not exist at all.

- forbid "transfer out" ("a player does not have the right to play cards or
influence minions in a way that will reduce his pool to 0 or less, or that
will greatly reduce his pool without giving him a chance to keep on playing"
or something like that).

And there is always the proposal I made before :

- A player must optimize his VPs at any given time, even to the point of
breaking any deal made in other circumstances : if these circumstances are
changed in any way, the deal is de facto considered invalid.

(of course, this one is more subjective, and I understand that in your PoV
it could break smaller, more subtle deals ; also, it takes deals into
account, and we all know they don't exist in the rules... ;).

Of course, these are just my 2-cents : I'm aware there's a big problem, and
like many here I try my best to come up with ways to correct it.

Now it's up to you and your team, if you wish, LSJ...

> - A player must optimize his VPs at any given time, even to the
> point of breaking any deal made in other circumstances : if these
> circumstances are changed in any way, the deal is de facto

Never mind the part of the rules addressing deals. If you have
the opportunity to go for a sure third victory point in a game
in which you'd already gotten two ousts, it shouldn't matter that
you may sacrifice fairly sizable chances at getting the sweep.
The biggest objective of a game in a tournament is to win the
game - period. That is the first and most important metric which
determine who makes the finals. Rules should not be created that,
if enforced, might risk a player his impending game win in the
interests of forcing him to go after a sweep.

Fred

> NEVER !! There is absolutely no valid reason for that. And read LSJ' lips :
> "There are no rules for deals". Which is part of the problem (there should
> be rules *against* deals). But you cannot be forced to respect something
> which doesn't exist, right ?

I am absolutely against rules against deals. They start endless
discussions about legal deals, they are mostly not judgeable and will
open all problems of collusions.

I agree that withdrawing should be abolished. You should not get the
same VPs for staying alive then for killing your prey. That sure would
make some dirty deals impossible.

If you accept that deals are part of the game, you can start the
possiblities to counter dirty deals in the game. 1st. Counter dealing.
Usually three players should be able to stop two players splitting the
table. 2nd. Making a better deal and breaking it. Like said before, if
you could exspect more deal breaking the dirty deals would get less.
(The Succubus Club deal is the classic example. Always accept it and
break it, will kill that deal in the long run.)

You got me thinking. How about this modification to the Game Win
tournament rule: After a given round the Game Win is awarded to the upper
25% of the players (meaning, that it is no longer necessarily tied to
exactly 3 VPs). Maybe calling it "Game Win" would no longer suffice...
This way people would no longer have a calculable cut-off point for the
preliminary rounds. It would not affect finals directly, though. I'm not
necessarily saying this is a good idea, as it would basically introduce
more competition between tables, but it would also introduce a certain
uncertainty that would make preliminary VP deals risky.

Bye,

Messages.Body:
"James Coupe" <ja...@zephyr.org.uk> wrote in message

news:3yhdpan...@newred.gradwell.net...

> "Orpheus" <orphe...@DEADSPAM.free.fr> writes:
>
> > I'm with you guys on this one. Nor do I think we're alone.
> > If there are really no rules / rulings about deals, there is
absolutely no
> > problem whatsoever, and people will know that a deal that isn't
anymore
> > mutually beneficial will be broken.
>
> If a deal is set-up such that the player is required to backstab the
> moment the deal becomes detrimental to him, no player will ever "go
> first" in a deal and therefore such deals cannot be made in the first
> place. This would prevent the game from generating subtly crafted
> deals of depth and intrigue. (There are many posts on Google about
> this, over time.)

Orpheus may have overstated a bit there. But what I do think might be
useful - and I disagree that the game wouldn't generate enough depth and
intrigue without as many deals, or as extensive deals, as it has now -
is a rule, like Orpheus and others have suggested, that players must
always attempt to get as many VPs as they reasonably can, regardless of
other circumstances. That is, that you cannot make (and keep) a deal
offering to not oust someone later in return for favors now. If you can
get more VPs, even if you have already won the game, you must do so.

I don't think that would eliminate most deals, since most deals (the
mutually beneficial "I help you a little, you help me a little" kind)
don't require anyone to promise to concede at the end of the game or
promise to allow withdrawing from the game.

I think the appropriate dividing line would not prohibit upholding a
deal to rescue someone's vampire instead of getting an oust this turn,
as long as you believe you'll still be able to get the oust next turn.
If you're not going to get the oust at all - ie you'll be ousted first
instead, or your prey will no longer be oustable - then you should get
the VP instead of upholding the deal. I think most people (who aren't
in the "death before dishonor!" camp) would not hold it against their
deal-partner to take this course of action when such a situation arises.
It is, after all, not a team game, and IMO it should have the maximum
reasonable incentives for players to not form teams.

Josh
