Messages.Author: James Coupe
Messages.Body:
"Frederick Scott" <dont...@mymail.com> writes:

> Also, I vaguely recall (read, "where my long-term memory is
> concerned, all bets are off!" :-P ) LSJ generally grouping
> anything involving outside acting on motivations that stem from
> sources outside the game - including such things as feeling that
> one needs only a single victory point to qualify for the finals
> and so playing to get one sure VP instead of a game win - under
> the collusion rule.

Leaving aside LSJ's rebuttal of his stance on this but...

The Collusion rules seem pretty clear - to me - that they are
referring to multiple players:
"Players agree to alter, predetermine, or otherwise illegally
establish the results of a game."

Compare, for instance, Cheating - Fraud:
"A player intentionally misrepresents rules, procedures, personal
information, or any other relevant tournament information."

Also, the "Play to Win" rules stem directly from the Sportsmanlike
Conduct requirements:

"That's what "play to win" means. Playing to win (i.e., not throwing a
game) is a small subset sportsmanlike conduct." [LSJ 20031014]
http://groups.google.com/groups?selm=3F8BE4A7.9000704%40white-wolf.com

So there is no need to bring into play Collusion as a ruling for 1VP
vs Game Win - the Sportsmanlike Conduct requirements can be applied to
the player. (Were I judging such, a verbal caution would probably be
applied first, before going any further.) And since there aren't - in
this case - multiple players involved, it's not Collusion, which
requires multiple players, by my reading.

Additionally, though somewhat as an aside, at least one form of
"outside sources" is *not* handled as Collusion. Cheating - Bribery
is one such instance. (Of course, were Collusion used for such
purposes as you describe, you could simply regard it as a catch all in
the absence of more specific points. This paragraph is mostly for
information, rather than rebutting your point.)

However, from the above, something like targeting a player because you
don't like them due to them being a deal breaker by a single person
would *not* be Collusion - Collusion requires more than one person, I
feel. So I'd rule it Unsportsmanlike Conduct.

And just adding more than one person to the situation doesn't - to my
mind - make it always Collusion. For instance, two players who commit
a Misrepresentation infraction, for instance, because they're both
convinced that the rules say that Lucita Clan Impersonating to
Lasombra makes her Sabbat wouldn't (necessarily!) be Collusion.

So, I'd be more inclined to just rule a multiple instance of
Unsportsmanlike Conduct.

Of course, as I've said, if there was some evidence to suggest that
the players had deliberately set out to, say, make the person lose
(rather than just 'teach them a lesson' or somesuch), I'd be much
happier to a move towards Collusion as a ruling.

In either event, I'd be unlikely to question a judge's ruling on the
issue either way, since it is their judgement as to which side of the
line such a thorny issue lies, and I *do* agree that such behaviour
needs to be dealt with. A judge being somewhat harsh (DQ rather than
Game Loss) or somewhat lenient (Game Loss rather than DQ) would be
unlikely to trouble me too much - they're both harsh penalties.

(Based on ruling it Unsportsmanlike Conduct - Major vs Collusion,
where Game Loss and DQ are the recommended penalties.)



Messages.Author: James Coupe
Messages.Body:
"Joshua Duffin" <duff...@bls.gov> writes:

> Orpheus may have overstated a bit there. But what I do think might be
> useful - and I disagree that the game wouldn't generate enough depth and
> intrigue without as many deals, or as extensive deals, as it has now -
> is a rule, like Orpheus and others have suggested, that players must
> always attempt to get as many VPs as they reasonably can, regardless of
> other circumstances. That is, that you cannot make (and keep) a deal
> offering to not oust someone later in return for favors now. If you can
> get more VPs, even if you have already won the game, you must do so.

The "Play to Win" rule can be - at least in part - determined based on
what a player does and if there was an openly made deal.

However, a rule of this kind either simply forbids actual words being
spoken, or requires the judge to be able to intervene about things
that weren't said - which is not an easy thing to do! That is, I can
ask players, spectators and ousted players if such a deal was actually
made currently. If there was one made, it all happens easily. If
there wasn't, I can rule play illegal. If there is dispute, I can ask
what each player thinks was said (and possibly ask a spectator or two
for assistance on this matter) and rule appropriately, based on what
seems reasonable from what people have said.

Now, we can simply prevent the words being said (and so this isn't a
VP splitting deal and move on). Or, if the judge has to intervene
based on things which weren't said, this is much harder to clear up.
I can't ask what *was* said. I have to ask what *wasn't* said. And
since there's no single point of reference for me to say "Was a deal
made?", I need to know what's gone on throughout the match.

This is Hard (tm).

Additionally, combine in the possibility for players to play badly
anyway, making mistakes, miscalculations and so forth... Was that
discussion earlier implying that I'd let myself be ousted, or have I
just screwed up in the late game?

As a judge, I'd rather be dealing with players who can play openly,
frankly and honestly. As a player, I'd rather such discussions were
open and honest, so I can combat them!

Providing an incentive for players to go undercover about such things
is... something I don't like.

> I don't think that would eliminate most deals, since most deals (the
> mutually beneficial "I help you a little, you help me a little" kind)
> don't require anyone to promise to concede at the end of the game or
> promise to allow withdrawing from the game.

The rule Orpheus proposed - backstabbing when it wasn't mutually
beneficial - does do that. It's not mutually beneficial for me to
spend time doing something that helps you and not me. As you say, it
is somewhat... overstated in its scope. (This is a big problem.)

Unless we accept that the fact that I *can* aid you in the future in
that fashion *does* aid me, because it gets your help.

From this, it is a small step to "I don't reasonably believe I can get
a TW, but I'm willing to help you get your TW if you aid me to getting
2VP out of it" - it's just the same principle, just on a larger scale.

(And those believing that this predetermines the fate of the game are
missing the point. Even in a deal which really, really, really isn't
a VP split deal, but long term mutual co-operation to prevent mutual
annihilation or stalling, it's in the interests of other players to
ally against this if they feel it's going to ruin their game. (If it
isn't going to ruin their game, it's not pre-determining the fate of
the game anyway.) If it is pre-determining the fate of the game, it
would be best to do something about it.)

> I think the appropriate dividing line would not prohibit upholding a
> deal to rescue someone's vampire instead of getting an oust this turn,
> as long as you believe you'll still be able to get the oust next turn.
> If you're not going to get the oust at all - ie you'll be ousted first
> instead, or your prey will no longer be oustable - then you should get
> the VP instead of upholding the deal. I think most people (who aren't
> in the "death before dishonor!" camp) would not hold it against their
> deal-partner to take this course of action when such a situation arises.
> It is, after all, not a team game, and IMO it should have the maximum
> reasonable incentives for players to not form teams.

My readings of many posts on this subject suggest that there are quite
a sizeable number of people who *would* hold it against their partner.
"You agreed to this and damnit, you broke your word. I'm never
speaking to you ever again." They may not be a majority, they may not
even be a large minority, but they certainly seem to be out there.
Bear in mind that not rescuing your vampire may mean that *you* die,
and some players area little tetchy about such things, even if you
were getting a VP out of the situation. (Add in a further complication
that if I save you now, you'll still be on the table for later play -
whereas letting you die might get me one VP, but prevent me from
getting any others because I want to bargain for your help to help me
vote someone down, or whatever.)

However, when you say "should get the VP instead if upholding the
deal", are you referring to sensible action on the part of the player,
or something that the "play to win" rules should enforce?

If the former, then I'd tend to agree - if it gets me a VP, I'd be
inclined to do it and apologise. But that's a personal play preference.

If we're saying that the player should - under the play to win rules -
have to take the VP now if they can't get it next turn, that's more
problematic.

First of all, what if I can't get them next turn but *could* get them
the turn after? For instance, if I don't oust them this turn, they'll
be able to get out Hasina Kesi as a blocker. (Say, I have a +1 bleed
vampire but have shown no stealth in my deck - my prey has gone
through my ash-heap to check this multiple times.) They have two
pool, so the one pool for Hasina Kesi isn't going to oust them. But
*I* know that I have Beast sitting down here, because I played
Effective Management this turn. (Or maybe he was just there.) So I
decide to send my +1 bleeder to rescue your vampire. 4 pool to Beast.

My prey brings out Hasina Kesi, ready to block me. My turn comes up.
I can't oust her, because I can't get past Hasina Kesi. But now I
transfer out Beast. The next-but-one turn, he rushes Hasina and then
I oust you.

Even without Beast, Hasina might block me, and then she taps the
following turn so I oust her - but she might be playing Wake, so I
can't oust her that turn.

And how reasonable will this belief have to be? If there's a Folderol
deck on the table, it could be doing cross-table reduction and, hey,
it might make a deal with the Hasina deck to keep it in, whilst it
gets a VP. (This table might be ordered Me - Hasina - Random Deck -
You - Folderol.) The Random deck might be troublesome in some way, so
the Folderol deck isn't unhappy to see it go away. (Anarch Revolt
deck, say - that's why the Hasina deck is in such trouble?) I might
not be able to oust you this turn, for that matter - so will I be
sacrificing *anything* if I rescue your vamp?

Or, perhaps, early on in the game, the Hasina deck was forced to play
with an open hand via Aura Reading. Or someone looked at the hand and
read out the cards in it (which might be lies, of course). If they'd
said "And she's got a Blood Doll", how reasonable is my belief? It
might not have been played, and if it is this turn, it'll get another
blood and... But the guy reading out the cards was lying.

A concrete "next but one" rule is therefore tricky, as is defining any
sort of reasonable belief.

And a judge coming along who has to rule "Yes, that play is legal"
when a player objects to it (saying they should be taking the oust!)
is going to be communicating a lot of information about a reasonable
assessment of the player's situation - whether we move it from a
concrete "next but one" to a "reasonable belief that they can still do
it" option, or not.

Whereas currently, a judge has to find out if a deal was made which
was reasonable at the time (and if it was debatable, another player
may well have called him across) and then allow or disallow the play
based on that.



Messages.Author: James Coupe
Messages.Body:
"Orpheus" <orphe...@DEADSPAM.free.fr> writes:

> No one knows how a situation on the game table can evolve, and there are
> often great surprises on what really happens a few turns after a given,
> apparently "frozen" gamestate. But the deals would certainly be more
> cautious, yes.

Read up to the first comma, and you'll see why a lot of your
objections to VP deals can go away.

No one knows how a situation on the game table can evolve. The table
split deal isn't a table split deal - it's two players attempting to
do that.

Since there are clearly still other player(s) on the table, there's
nothing to stop them from intervening in this cosy little arrangement.

Of course, some players just curl up in a ball and say "Oh no, table
split deal! Woe! Alas! I'm doomed! The future is written in
stone!" They lose, based on the other players being better at
exploiting that facet of the game than them.

> Still, I disagree : the game can be just as subtle without table-split
> deals. Keep in mind that this is what we're talking again here.

But... you can't define what a table-split deal *is*.

So how do you propose to remove them from the game?

> > Whilst it would be difficult to rule in a case of minor dealing over
> > little bits of play of minor consequence, a general principle of "You
> > must break a deal if it's in your interest" would apply to those too.
>
> It may be in your interest to respect a small deal, and a judge has very few
> means to evaluate that, nor does he has the right to tell a player how to
> play.

It may be in my interests to respect a much larger deal that we made, too!

If I can't get any VPs at all currently, respecting the larger deal
that gets me one or two VPs is in my interests.

> But if deals look like collusion, or a non-optimisation of Vps, he can judge
> and deal accordingly.

If it's collusion, sure. But collusion is nothing to do with table
splits. Collusion is a specific form of cheating. Table split/VP
split deals are not collusion, so I'm unsure why you raise it here -
collusion is illegal, everyone agrees on that.

Non-optimisation of VPs is - as discussed elsewhere - extremely tricky
to define. Bad play, for instance. Does the judge have to step in
there? And if there is a deal and you do, honestly, play badly when
trying to carry it out, why should the judge have to intervene to
correct an honest bad play?

(Now extend this to the judge having to decide if something is an
honest bad play or not. Bear in mind that some players have terrific
poker faces and a judge who is good at many aspects of the game may be
bad at reading poker faces.)

> > Or is there some threshold over which a deal of that sort would be
> > measured and things under the radar need not be examined? Would you
> > care to define the general principle of when a player can keep a deal,
> > even though they might be able to do something better with that minion
> > (e.g. oust their prey instead of rescuing your vampire from torpor),
> > and when they can't?

[snip - short term interest, choices and timing]

> Or bad play (I know a player who doesn't bleed to kill his prey and looses
> games he should win ; just because he panics). But the judge should be able
> to determine which one it is.

"Should be able to determine" is different from "Is able to determine".

I can think of, without even trying, one player I've judged who seems
to spend every tournament I've been at swinging between good play and
shocking (in my view) mistakes. These aren't mistakes related to
deals, necessarily. Just completely misjudging (again, in my view)
what s/he should be doing next.

If I see a bad play from him/her during the upholding of a deal I
might need to intervene on, does he get more leeway than other
players?

If s/he does, that's a problem. Legbiter has posited the
psychological aspects of making deliberate, but plausible, mistakes.
(Including Thrown Sewer Lid in a low-but-not-zero potence Toreador
deck.) If players can now get tangible judging benefits from making
innocuous mistakes...

If s/he doesn't, then how am I to rule which it is? I know s/he makes
mistakes, I've seen it. But if I can't give him/her leeway, it's not
a question of judging which it is - it's a question of upholding some
standard of play below which I have to intervene. Which is obviously
problematic!

> And all of us who had to judge deals know that the guidelines are just that,
> and that ultimately it's the you, your logic and your conscience (there are
> no rules about deals).

A player may uphold a deal that was legally made, even if making the
deal again right now wouldn't be legal due to a change in
circumstances.

LSJ has spelled that out quite a few times. It's not a "rule" per se,
but it's just as much a rule as any other ruling or interpretation he
makes.

If the deal was legal when it was made (in your reasonable judgement),
it's legal to uphold it. This isn't necessarily simple to determine,
but it's a very simple explanation of the subject.

(I'm unsure where "conscience" comes into it. I'm not doing anything
bad or wrong. I'm just making a judgment on whether I think something
is reasonable or not. Possibly a translation issue.)

> Hoping this will help you understand our viewpoint,

It's not a question of viewpoint. You don't like VP split deals. I
get that.

What you don't get is that what you propose - regardless of its
suitability or otherwise (which is also being discussed) - is highly
impractical. You're asking for judges to read minds.



Messages.Author: Frederick Scott
Messages.Body:
"Orpheus" <orphe...@DEADSPAM.free.fr> wrote in message

news:41623f63$0$29157$626a...@news.free.fr...

> > Never mind the part of the rules addressing deals. If you have
> > the opportunity to go for a sure third victory point in a game
> > in which you'd already gotten two ousts, it shouldn't matter that
> > you may sacrifice fairly sizable chances at getting the sweep.
> > The biggest objective of a game in a tournament is to win the
> > game - period. That is the first and most important metric which
> > determine who makes the finals. Rules should not be created that,
> > if enforced, might risk a player his impending game win in the
> > interests of forcing him to go after a sweep.
>
> It is obvious that risking losing the GW to get more VPs isn't
> optimizing !!

But trying to create a rule around making people "optimize their
VPs" doesn't actually say that. If you allow for a heirarchy of
motivations - which is what you're doing - it becomes fuzzy when
people need to be going for the one and when they must start taking
the other into account. The only really concrete thing that can
be accomplished without screwing anything up is to say that once
a player has already acheived a game win for sure, then he should
continue to go after as many extra VPs as he can get. But that
shouldn't say anything about VPs he'd agreed to give away in order
to nail down the game win.

> But then, I'll tell you that gaining more VPs also is a way to get
> into the finals

It can be sometimes. But game wins are always the most important
thing. A game win is worth more than infinity VPs.

> Furthermore, I believe that calculating the number of VPs you need /
> already have is an out-of-game consideration, right LSJ ?

That has nothing to do with anything. This issue is a thing that
comes up when you suspect a player of *sacrificing* his chance at
a game win because you suspect he's only going for a set number of
victory points. Doesn't work the other way around. If a player
wants to go after a game win *instead* of optimizing his victory
points, that's OK. In fact, current rules say that's what he's
supposed to be doing. (Or such is my understanding.)

Fred

> victory points. Doesn't work the other way around. If a player
> wants to go after a game win *instead* of optimizing his victory
> points, that's OK. In fact, current rules say that's what he's
> supposed to be doing. (Or such is my understanding.)

They do.

A player is never - for instance - required to play for a potentially
difficult table sweep when they could play for a much more reasonable
3 VP TW. (Compare an F1 racing driver; he wants to come first but
isn't under any rules-based pressure to have as big a lead as humanly
possible, which may risk him crashing.)

Of course, the reverse is pretty much true, since they're still
playing to win.

As is typically useful, the judge trying to explain to a player
"You're not allowed to win that way" (barring collusion,
unsportsmanlike conduct etc.) is largely avoided.

> There are long long looooong discussions when deals are being made. Since deal making
> is not supported by the rules, shouldn't a long discussion (aribitrary criteria to
> determine whether a discussion is "long", yes I know) be stopped and called stalling?

In fact, LSJ's interpretation of the "play to win" rules have long
accounted for various forms of deals. The "The rules say nothing
about deals" side of the argument is technically true but not entirely
useful.

However, if you look at the examples for Cheating - Stalling we get:

"(A) A player has no options available to significantly affect the
game, and spends several minutes "thinking" about what to do."

If a player really has no options, the deal will probably not take
very long at all. (And lengthy discussions of "Well, should I hunt
with him first or him? And which will you give me more help over?"
will quite possibly be declared stalling.)

If a player has several significant options available to him,
discussing with another player as to which is best to achieve mutually
beneficial goals seems to run counter to this example.

Additionally, Stalling is:

"A player intentionally plays slowly in order to take advantage of the
time limit."

Making a lengthy deal may well have nothing to do with the time limit
at all. (It would be hard, for instance, to decide that a long
discussion at 30 minutes into the game was trying to take advantage of
this.) A "Slow Play" infraction might be appropriate if the players
really are taking a lot of time discussing nothing, but Stalling is
generally something more devious, IMO.

Yeah, I'm really tired of playing games of V:TES that include the words
"... or I'll transfer out." What the fuck? Play the game. Nobody is
here to let you win; they all want to win themselves. Not in a winning
position? Build your deck better, or play better.

I'll be the first to admit that I've used it too, and I'm not really
proud of that fact. At the same time, I'm fully behind the "remove this
bullshit from the game" perspective. I've proposed a simple rule
before, and I'll repeat it:

"You may not spend pool that would reduce you below 1."

This does not stop you from calling an Anarchist Uprising and nuking
yourself and your prey for a VP. This does not stop you from
transferring yourself to 1 and refusing to block. But it does stop you
from:

-- transferring your last pool
-- blowing through the straw to a Blood Doll
-- playing a Master that costs exactly what you have left
-- playing an action card whose cost is exactly what you have left
-- etcetera

The biggest problem is, as always, the "out of turn 6 pool" that
happens, which screws the grandpredator of the self-nukee. Someone who
chooses not to defend themselves cannot be stopped; they can fake it
effectively. But you can force their predator to do the last point of
damage, which stops a whole lot of the "I will transfer myself out"
bullshit.

-- Derek

Every move you take 'unbalances the table'.

Example: a player with a rush deck is in a lost position. He is down to one
pool, has no pool gain available, his prey has more pool than he can take
and there is one (or one dozen) AR on the table while his predator has
absolute control of the votes. What should he do?
a) transfer out
b) rush or bleed his prey
c) rush his predator
d) do nothing.

Your ruling would prevent a), but any other option will have an effect on
the remaining game. There is no 'bad play' here, he is going to be ousted
whatever he does, how can one play be ruled worse than the other in that
situation?
Wether any option he takes is unsportsmanlike depends on his intentions, not
on the specific action he is taking.

Flux

Ousting a player is (usually) not the result of a single action, but of a
set of actions taken during a whole game. Why should it be required that
last of those actions is taken by the predator, yet all other previous
actions might be taken by the player himself (due to bad play, for example)?

not matter.

You quote two-player games as an example, which are not directly
comparable. I suggest identifying a multiplayer game if you're going to
use this angle.

If I resign in Chess, my opponent wins a 100% win, and absolutely nobody
else in the current game is affected by this. Same with Go.

If I resign (transfer out) in V:TES, my predator gets a partial win
(1VP), and the rest of the table is significantly affected.

When used in the sense Tet is thinking, it is. Threatening suicide from

I've seen it plenty; a player who is capable of defending and whose game
is far from over, but chooses instead to try to extort favors from the

predator". Bah. I've seen variants of it too (related to "I'll oust

>You almost oust your prey, but your prey has all but ousted her own prey
>who is moreover in a lost position. Why force that prey to choose only from

Ah, this is not necessarily an accurate statement of the situation.

Start at 9 pool.

-- Play Master costing 2 pool
-- Push 1 through Blood Doll.
-- Bleed for 1 with each minion, or hunt, tapping out
-- Transfer 4, leaving self at 2, announce "I don't block anything."

A different set of choices leaves this player at 9, maybe even 10 pool,
and in a very un-lost position. But I have seen the above (or similar)
happen far too many times. Granted, this does not provide the same "out
of turn VP", but you can't tell me that this isn't a disruptive,
unsportsmanlike play.

>the set of plays which gives her VP to you instead of her predator (your

You wish to encourage kingmaking that much?

A prey in a truly lost position shouldn't be allowed to affect the game
in such a significant fashion. It's even worse when the prey in
question isn't actually in a lost position.

>prey). Clearly I can see why the "you" in that scenario would prefer that
>he not be allowed to, but just as clearly the "your prey" in that scenario
>would be happy to ban the use of Life Boon, for example, in those
>circumstances, instead.

Life Boon must be in your hand, in your deck, and you must have enough
pool to play it without getting ousted yourself. I'm not happy when
someone Life Boons my prey either, but it's an effect that's part of the
game and it has plenty of actual cost and opportunity cost.

What Life Boon ISN'T is an attempt to completely circumvent the
mechanics of the game in an effort to compensate for poor deckbuilding,
poor play, or perhaps just plain old bad luck.

>Anyone would be happier in general with more VPs than with fewer.

That's not the point, and I know you also have seen the above scenario
played out, both on a table near you and probably on a table with you at
some point.

The point is that the card-play should be the primary factor in
determining who gets the more VPs, and who gets the fewer; not someone
deciding to just give up and kingmake.

>And what's keeping your from making the deal and then ousting your new prey
>anyhow (again, in the more fully developed example from Tet's post)?

What if the "let me get a VP" involves you having to provide immediate
favors before you get a chance to break that deal?

Besides, too many people will honor those deals, even though it's not
one that deserves to be paid a speck of attention. It's not that it's
necessarily ME in the grandpredator situation; I'm disgusted with it no
matter where I sit at the table, or if I'm standing next to the table,
or whatever.

>Build your deck better, or play better (to put more pressure on your prey
>so
>her own prey doesn't get so weak in the first place, or backstab for a
>sweep,
>either way).

The scenario above should demonstrate that it's not possible to build a
deck that can not only oust its prey consistently, but can even do so
when its grandprey deliberately attempts to lose, AND a deck that can
even manage a GW under these circumstances. Not to mention survive
against the cross-table hostilities that ensue whenever anyone plays
well.

I build my decks with the intent of playing the game. It seems patently
obvious that some others don't do the same.

>>

No? It sure looks like spending to me. Fortunately, we have this thing
called "rulings" that allows a person with sufficient authority to
declare that moving counters from your pool to the blood bank, or onto a
card in play (Powerbase: Washington, Secret Horde), will be considered
"spending" for purposes of this rule.

We can quibble about the exact wording later. For now, the intent
itself is what is on the table.

>> -- playing a Master that costs exactly what you have left
>> -- playing an action card whose cost is exactly what you have left
>> -- etcetera
>>
>> The biggest problem is, as always, the "out of turn 6 pool" that
>> happens, which screws the grandpredator of the self-nukee. Someone who

>> [bunk].
>

>-- Cycling a card that would cost your last pool under an agreement to

I've personally never seen this. Ever.

> cycling itself was still my best/only option for more VPs.

Sure. But you've done this exactly once, and I've never seen it, and
I'm sure the vast majority of people have neither done nor seen it also.

You don't acknowledge corner-case examples as valid when people question
you about rulings; I don't think I should acknowledge the above
corner-case example as mattering in this case, either. :) I know that
I see a lot more threats to transfer out (from varying situations) than
I do either of these two counterexamples you've held up.

>-- Playing Archon Investigation when you'd be ousted either way.

I approve of this being removed from the game, since it's a
burn-that-minion effect. If you're gone, you're gone; don't go for the
spite-bone on your way out.

The case only applies when you happen to have exactly three pool,
anyway, so it falls under the same corner-case situation as above; if
you have 2 pool, you can't even play AI, and if you have 4 pool, you can

The game is certainly complex. Some of the rules are also complex, as a
result. This one would be pretty clear in its intent, albeit with a
certain degree of complexity.

When does a good player transfers himself out. (so i am not talking
about unsportsmanlike/colussion self ousting):

- He will die (usually by a deal) and wants to honour his predator
ally.

- His prey made more pressure on him than was necessary. (For example
killing all his vampires even he was no S&B deck) He would stay
forever with his pool but would do nothing (and not winning any VP).
With self-ousting he can punish the bad play of his prey.

- A trick deck played by his grand predator (usually with swapping
seating order or with breaking a deal) wants to make a sweep and kill
his predator and him in a row. He doesnt want to reward that play, so
he ousts himself to help his predator. Its his last possiblity to be
an active part of the game.

Are these really cases we should stop by forbidding self-ousting.

Transfering out is only one option that will influence the table, it's no
better or worse than any other.

Going back to my 'dead rush deck' from another post, let's say that each
player has only one minion left.
If the player choses to transfer out, both prey and predator can still play
the game afterwards. If he rushes either one, he can kill that player's
game. Which option is less intrusive?
He can also do nothing, but how do you rule that a player may not take any
action at all when in a lost position, and why should you rule that?

If the game is far from over, call the judge, and if in his opinion the
player has plenty of valid options to play on with a good chance, the judge
will block the self-oust.

If the game isn't far from over, and the threat is real, either accept the
implicit deal, or let the guy go down in flames.

If he's a puppet for his predator, who keeps him around at low pool, oust
him yourself.

I don't have to like it either, but there are more types of play I don't
particularly appreciate. Part of the game, though, and I'll deal with them
as they arise.

>>You almost oust your prey, but your prey has all but ousted her own prey

>>from

> happen far too many times. Granted, this does not provide the same "out
> of turn VP", but you can't tell me that this isn't a disruptive,
> unsportsmanlike play.

I'd call it disruptive and unsportsmanlike, yes. (Especially if the player
intends to go through with this).

However, I believe there's at least one strategy article that espouses the
view that you can 'milk' the table for favors when you're being hurt or low
on pool - and who's to say (from observing the table) that's not actually
the tactic that's going on? (Until the player indeed does not block and lets
himself be ousted).

I personally consider no game lost until my last pool is removed and so will
very likely not self-oust - but if I can get table-love from threatening to
self-oust, why not try? (And occasionally I'll be forced to back up my
threat or lose credibility - I'll decide at that point which is worth more
to me. However, you could say, that given the tournament rule to go for
maximal VP in the current game, disregarding all other games, this threat is
neccesarily hollow).

>>the set of plays which gives her VP to you instead of her predator (your
>
> You wish to encourage kingmaking that much?
>
> A prey in a truly lost position shouldn't be allowed to affect the game
> in such a significant fashion. It's even worse when the prey in
> question isn't actually in a lost position.

If the player isn't actually in a lost position, he should play for maximal
VPs. You cannot legislate against bad play nor play his deck for him,
though.

If the player is in a truly lost position, he's free to go out any way he
likes - including cross-table shenannigans. If there's a player cross-table
who could've given you 2 pool each turn, and 3 turns ago you told him: "if
you don't give me that 2 pool each turn, I will torporise 2 of your guys
before dying", why shouldn't you be allowed to follow up on that threat?

(I can, of course, still sympathise with any player that feels like he's
been screwed by spite or by bad or uncaring cross-table play - which
includes death-throes weirdness.)

>>And what's keeping your from making the deal and then ousting your new
>>prey
>>anyhow (again, in the more fully developed example from Tet's post)?
>

Then that's the risk you take.

> or whatever.

Like I've said before, I agree with this. Too many deals that should be
broken are kept, sometimes due to lack of insight, sometimes due to 'honor
system'.

>>Build your deck better, or play better (to put more pressure on your prey
>>so
>>her own prey doesn't get so weak in the first place, or backstab for a
>>sweep,
>>either way).

> well.
>

> obvious that some others don't do the same.

Perhaps those deckbuilders (validly) see 'playing the game' as being the
whole set of options available to them - including deal-making.

>>It also stops you from:
>>-- Cycling a card that would cost your last pool under an agreement to
>> have your grand-predator (or whoever) cancel it (Sudden or DI). I've
>
> I've personally never seen this. Ever.

I've been asked by players from a table in the recent ECQ if this cycle
method would be possible (they were concerned about the blood being spent
and then retrieved instead of not being spent at all), but the master
thought to cost 2 pool cost 1 pool instead, so there was no issue. If it HAD
cost 2 pool they might have cycled this way.

Tobias
Deventer

I'm sure that LSJ is aware that what you seem to be looking for is
some kind of precedent casebook for making judgements.

The problem is that any specific guidelines would be contingent upon
the game state.

So, you are asking LSJ to define some game states, which (for
non-trivial cases) will be huge documents that are very time consuming
to prepare, check etc. Of course, LSJ is (presumably) paid to prepare
resources for VTES, but I would rather he spent his time thinking
about the rules and designing new sets.

Even if he did prepare a casebook his examples will be next to useless
as a guideline, as it is very unlikely that his example game states
would be replicated precisely in your particular play. How to
interpret his example as a guide to your situation will merely result
in a Big Argument, which will finally result in relying on the judge
making a judgement (exactly the situation we have at the moment,
anyway).

All that specific guidelines will do is give ammunition to rules
lawyer sorts who will try and finesse judgements in the casebook to
their advantage (see any legal system based on precedent).

* lehrbuch

Messages.Author: Andrew S. Davidson
Messages.Body:
On Mon, 04 Oct 2004 10:37:03 GMT, LSJ wrote:

>The judge cannot masquerade behind the
>stalling rule to undermine legal play that
>she finds distasteful.

This need not arise as, happily, the VEKN has a rule forbidding slow
play per se, i.e. "5.3. Slow Play". This section forbids not only
stalling but also "playing excessively slowly". Since deal making is
not sanctioned by the rules, then taking time out to discuss deals is
always excessive - i.e. additional to the time required to simply play
one's cards. A judge is therefore entitled to curtail any and all
conversation of this sort unless it is conducted in parallel with the
play of the cards and so does not delay the game.

And this not just a theoretical consideration. Tournament games often
run out of time, right? And players are spending periods of 5 minutes
to an hour discussing deals, right? The Slow Play rule is there so
that games are played in a timely manner and so finish in the time
allowed. Judges, do your duty!

Andrew
